front: A 40-year-old male undergoes a gastric secretory test. The administration of a specific hormone significantly increases pepsinogen secretion while inhibiting HCl production. Name this hormone.
back: Secretin. • Inhibits parietal cell HCl activity. • Stimulates chief cells to release pepsinogen. • Triggered by acid entering the duodenum.

category: Elaborate the metabolic effects of these hormones
front: Detail the mechanism by which Gastrin-Releasing Peptide (GRP) influences gastric acid production.
back: • Released from vagal nerve endings. • Directly stimulates G cells in the antrum to secrete Gastrin. • Indirectly increases HCl via Gastrin-ECL-Parietal axis.

category: Elaborate the metabolic effects of these hormones
front: Differentiate the metabolic effects of Insulin and Enterogastrone on gastric acid secretion.
back: • Insulin: Increases HCl secretion indirectly by inducing hypoglycemia-mediated vagal stimulation. • Enterogastrone: Inhibits both HCl secretion and gastric motility.

category: Elaborate the metabolic effects of these hormones
front: Identify the co-transmitter released alongside acetylcholine in salivary glands that mediates vasodilation during secretory activity.
back: VIP (Vasoactive Intestinal Polypeptide). • Causes local vasodilation to support energy-dependent saliva formation. • Also inhibits gastric acid secretion in the stomach.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: A clinical condition characterized by a gastrin-secreting tumor leading to severe refractory peptic ulcers and hyperchlorhydria is known as [___].
back:
• Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome.
• Characterized by excess Gastrin.
• Leads to severe acidic injury of the duodenum.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: A patient presents with fat malabsorption, steatorrhea, and failure of the gallbladder to contract during a meal. Which hormone's deficiency is most likely responsible?
back:
• Cholecystokinin (CCK).
• Essential for pancreatic enzyme secretion.
• Stimulates gallbladder contraction and relaxes the Sphincter of Oddi.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: Explain the biological function of Somatostatin in terms of its inhibitory role in the stomach.
back:
• Inhibits Gastrin release from G-cells.
• Directly inhibits parietal cell HCl secretion.
• Acts as a universal 'off switch' for GIT hormones.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: Distinguish between the consequences of Secretin deficiency versus Gastrin excess regarding the duodenal environment.
back:
• Secretin deficiency: Failure to neutralize acid due to poor bicarbonate secretion.
• Gastrin excess: Overwhelming acid load beyond buffering capacity.
• Result: Both cause duodenal ulceration.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: Identify the key symptoms of a Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP) secreting tumor (VIPoma).
back:
• Watery Diarrhea.
• Hypokalemia.
• Achlorhydria (WDHA syndrome).
• Profound metabolic consequences due to excess intestinal secretion.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: The deficiency of [___], a glycoprotein secreted by parietal cells, leads to Pernicious Anemia due to Vitamin B12 malabsorption.
back:
• Intrinsic Factor.
• Specifically required for B12 absorption in the distal ileum.
• Deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neurological symptoms.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: In a patient with chronic Achlorhydria, there is excessive bacterial growth in the stomach. Which specific organic acid rises in the gastric juice as a marker of this condition?
back:
• Lactic Acid.
• Reflects bacterial fermentation in the absence of HCl.
• Associated with gastric carcinoma or chronic atrophic gastritis.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: Describe the physiological cause of the 'Dumping Syndrome' seen after a total gastrectomy.
back:
• Loss of stomach's reservoir function.
• Rapid entry of hyperosmolar food into the small intestine.
• Causes sudden fluid shifts, serotonin release, and abdominal distension.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: Contrast the effects of Gastrin and Secretin on gastric motility and acid secretion.
back:
• Gastrin: Stimulates motility and HCl secretion.
• Secretin: Inhibits motility and HCl secretion (acts as an enterogastrone).
• Secretin stimulates bicarbonate secretion from the pancreas.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: Identify the primary hormone responsible for the alkaline tide and its role in neutralizing acidic chyme entering the duodenum.
back:
• Secretin.
• Stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretion.
• Released by S-cells in response to duodenal pH dropping below 4.5.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: Hypersecretion of Gastrin, typically caused by a gastrinoma, leads to the clinical condition known as [___] Syndrome, characterized by severe, refractory peptic ulcers.
back: Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome. Key points: Massive HCl production by parietal cells; Multiple ulcers in atypical locations; Persistent diarrhea/steatorrhea due to lipase inactivation.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: A 45-year-old male presents with chronic malabsorption and foul-smelling, greasy stools. If the underlying cause is a deficiency in Cholecystokinin (CCK) release, the pathophysiology involves a failure to stimulate [___].
back: Pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction. Key points: CCK is released by I-cells in response to fats/proteins; Stimulates acinar cells; Necessary for fat emulsification and digestion.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: Explain the physiological consequence of a deficiency in Secretin upon the entry of acidic chyme into the duodenum.
back: Failure of acid neutralization. Key points: Reduced pancreatic bicarbonate (HCO3-) secretion; Sustained low duodenal pH; Inactivation of pancreatic enzymes and duodenal mucosal injury.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: A patient is diagnosed with a Somatostatinoma (excess somatostatin). Contrast the effect of this excess on Gastrin levels versus its effect on pancreatic exocrine function.
back: Inhibitory on both. Key points: Suppresses Gastrin (causing hypochlorhydria); Inhibits CCK/Secretin (causing pancreatic insufficiency and steatorrhea); Results in global G.I. secretory shutdown.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
coreConcept: Intrinsic Factor and Vitamin B12 absorption
front: The gastric glycoprotein required for Vitamin B12 absorption in the ileum, whose deficiency leads to pernicious anemia, is [___].
back: * Intrinsic Factor.* Deficiency prevents Vitamin B12 uptake in the distal ileum.* Results in megaloblastic (pernicious) anemia.* It is the only gastric function essential for life.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: A patient presents with multiple recurrent peptic ulcers and high serum gastrin levels. Name the underlying condition and the hormone in excess.
back: * Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome.* Hormone in excess is Gastrin.* Hypergastrinemia causes massive HCl secretion by parietal cells.* Leads to severe mucosal injury and treatment-resistant ulceration.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: Explain the primary physiological consequence when Secretin fails to be released in response to acidic chyme entering the duodenum.
back: * Failure to stimulate pancreatic bicarbonate secretion.* Loss of neutralization of acidic chyme in the duodenum.* Inactivation of pancreatic digestive enzymes (optimum pH 8.0).* Increased risk of duodenal ulceration.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: Contrast the effects of Gastrin and Somatostatin on gastric acid (HCl) secretion.
back: * Gastrin: Potent stimulator of HCl release via ECL cell histamine induction.* Somatostatin: Potent universal inhibitor.* Somatostatin antagonizes the stimulatory effects of gastrin, histamine, and acetylcholine to prevent hyperacidity.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: Predict the clinical outcome of a deficiency in Cholecystokinin (CCK) regarding lipid digestion.
back: * Impaired gallbladder contraction and bile release.* Reduced secretion of pancreatic lipase and co-lipase.* Results in fat malabsorption and steatorrhea (fatty, foul-smelling stools).

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: The inhibitory hormone that reduces the secretion of almost all other GIT hormones and gastric acid when present in excess is [___].
back: * Somatostatin.* Functions as a paracrine and endocrine inhibitor.* Secreted by D-cells in the stomach, pancreas, and intestine.* Excess inhibits gastrin, secretin, and CCK release.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: A patient is diagnosed with Achlorhydria (total absence of HCl). Describe the primary protective and digestive consequences.
back: * Loss of antiseptic action leading to gastric microbial overgrowth.* Failure to activate pepsinogen to pepsin, impairing protein digestion.* Reduced iron absorption due to failure to convert ferric to ferrous iron.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: Describe the "WDHA" syndrome associated with a VIP-secreting tumor (VIPoma).
back: * Watery Diarrhea, Hypokalemia, and Achlorhydria.* VIP stimulates massive intestinal water/electrolyte secretion.* Simultaneously inhibits gastric acid production.* Results in severe dehydration and electrolyte imbalances.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: Contrast the primary roles of GIP and Secretin in GIT physiology.
back: * GIP: Acts as an incretin to stimulate insulin release and inhibits gastric acid/motility.* Secretin: Primary role is stimulating pancreatic bicarbonate for chyme neutralization.* Both inhibit gastric acid secretion but have different primary targets.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: Identify the physiological consequence of excessive salivary Kallikrein activity.
back: * Excessive Bradykinin production.* Causes profound local vasodilation.* Leads to significantly increased blood flow to the salivary glands during periods of high secretory activity.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: In the condition of Achlorhydria, the complete absence of [___] leads to increased microbial growth and elevated lactic acid levels in the gastric juice.
back: ● Hydrochloric acid (HCl). ● HCl provides essential antiseptic action in the stomach. ● Absence allows bacterial fermentation of food residues, producing lactic acid.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: A patient presents with multiple peptic ulcers and severe diarrhea. Labs show extremely high serum gastrin levels. Explain the hormonal mechanism causing the ulcers.
back: ● Hypergastrinemia (Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome). ● Excess gastrin overstimulates parietal cells via H2/CCK2 receptors. ● Massive HCl hypersecretion overwhelms the protective gastric and duodenal mucosal barriers.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: Explain how a deficiency in Secretin secretion affects the pH of the duodenal contents after a meal.
back: ● Prevents stimulation of bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice. ● Fails to neutralize acidic chyme entering from the stomach. ● Results in a persistently low (acidic) duodenal pH, increasing ulcer risk.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
coreConcept: Intrinsic Factor vs. Dietary B12 Deficiency
front: Contrast the clinical consequences of Vitamin B12 deficiency caused by a total gastrectomy versus a simple dietary lack.
back: ● Gastrectomy: Loss of Intrinsic Factor prevents B12 absorption in the ileum (Pernicious Anemia). ● Dietary: Insufficient intake despite functional absorption. ● Both result in megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: Describe the metabolic consequence of excess Aldosterone on the electrolyte composition of saliva.
back: ● Stimulates Na+ and Cl- reabsorption from salivary ducts. ● Increases K+ secretion into the duct lumen. ● Results in saliva with very low Na+ and high K+ concentrations.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: Chronic fat malabsorption and steatorrhea may result from a deficiency of [___], the hormone responsible for stimulating gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme release.
back: ● Cholecystokinin (CCK). ● CCK ensures bile and lipases reach the duodenum for fat digestion. ● Deficiency leads to failure of fat emulsification and hydrolysis.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: A patient presents with 'Dumping Syndrome' following gastric surgery. Which hormonal deficiency contributes to the rapid entry of hyperosmolar food into the small intestine?
back: ● Deficiency of Enterogastrone (GIP/Secretin). ● Loss of inhibitory feedback that normally slows gastric emptying. ● Rapid transit causes osmotic diarrhea, nausea, and palpitations.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: How does an excess of Somatostatin, as seen in somatostatinomas, affect the overall process of digestion?
back: ● Universal inhibition of GI hormones (Gastrin, CCK, Secretin). ● Suppresses pancreatic enzyme, bile, and acid secretion. ● Leads to steatorrhea, gallstones, and achlorhydria due to general GI suppression.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
coreConcept: HCl Role in Ulcers and Iron Absorption
front: Contrast the impact of HCl excess on the duodenum versus the impact of HCl deficiency on iron absorption.
back: ● Excess: Causes duodenal ulcers by overwhelming mucosal defenses. ● Deficiency: Impairs iron absorption by failing to convert ferric (Fe3+) to the easily absorbable ferrous (Fe2+) state.

category: Infer the consequences of deficiency and excess of these hormones
front: Describe the consequence of a deficiency in the salivary enzyme Lysozyme on oral hygiene.
back: ● Loss of natural antibacterial protection. ● Increased bacterial growth and food residue accumulation. ● Results in higher incidence of dental caries and foul breath (halitosis).

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: The primary rate-limiting and committed step of the glycolytic pathway is the conversion of fructose 6-phosphate to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, catalyzed by [___].
back:
• Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1)
• Allosterically activated by AMP and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate
• Inhibited by high ATP and Citrate levels
• Most important control point of the pathway

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: A laboratory technician collects blood in a tube containing sodium fluoride to measure plasma glucose. Sodium fluoride prevents glucose consumption by inhibiting which specific glycolytic enzyme?
back:
• Enolase
• Fluoride binds magnesium ions, a required cofactor
• Competes for the enzyme active site
• Preserves glucose levels for accurate diagnostic testing

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: Describe the mechanism by which Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate (F-2,6-BP) influences hepatic glycolysis during the well-fed state.
back:
• Potently activates PFK-1 allosterically
• Overcomes inhibition caused by high ATP
• Synthesized by PFK-2 in response to high insulin/glucagon ratio
• Reciprocally inhibits gluconeogenesis via Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: Contrast the kinetic properties (Km and Vmax) and tissue distribution of Glucokinase versus Hexokinase.
back:
• Glucokinase: High Km (low affinity), High Vmax, Liver/Pancreatic beta cells, Not inhibited by G6P
• Hexokinase: Low Km (high affinity), Low Vmax, Most extrahepatic tissues, Inhibited by G6P
• Glucokinase acts as a glucose sensor

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: Outline the biological significance and net ATP yield of anaerobic glycolysis in mature erythrocytes.
back:
• Significance: Sole energy source as RBCs lack mitochondria
• Net Yield: 2 ATP per glucose molecule
• End Product: Lactate
• Maintains ion pumps and biconcave cell shape

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: In the Rapoport-Luebering Shunt within erythrocytes, the intermediate 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate is converted to [___] to facilitate oxygen unloading to tissues.
back:
• 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG)
• Decreases Hemoglobin's affinity for Oxygen
• Shifts the oxygen-dissociation curve to the right
• Costs the cell one potential ATP generation step

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: A 4-year-old child presents with chronic hemolytic anemia and splenomegaly. Labs show decreased ATP and increased 2,3-BPG in erythrocytes. Which enzyme deficiency explains this pathophysiology?
back:
• Pyruvate Kinase (PK) deficiency
• Second most common RBC enzyme deficiency
• Lack of ATP causes ion pump failure and cell lysis
• High 2,3-BPG levels help compensate for anemia

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: Explain the specific reactions in glycolysis where energy is conserved via substrate-level phosphorylation.
back:
• 1,3-Bisphosphoglycerate to 3-Phosphoglycerate (Phosphoglycerate Kinase)
• Phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to Pyruvate (Pyruvate Kinase)
• Direct transfer of high-energy phosphate to ADP
• Occurs twice per glucose molecule (4 ATP total produced)

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: Distinguish between the fate of NADH in aerobic versus anaerobic glycolysis.
back:
• Aerobic: NADH is oxidized in the mitochondria via Electron Transport Chain (yields ~3 ATP)
• Anaerobic: NADH is oxidized by Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) in the cytosol
• Regenerates NAD+ required for continued glycolysis

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: State the significance of the first irreversible step in glycolysis catalyzed by Hexokinase/Glucokinase.
back:
• Traps glucose inside the cell as Glucose 6-Phosphate
• Polar phosphate group prevents diffusion across membrane
• Lowers intracellular free glucose to maintain concentration gradient
• Not the committed step (G6P used in other pathways)

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: The rate-limiting and most important regulatory step of the glycolytic pathway is the conversion of Fructose 6-phosphate to Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate by the enzyme [___].
back:
Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1).
- Activated by AMP and Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate.
- Inhibited by ATP and Citrate.
- Represents the 'committed' step of glycolysis.

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: A 4-year-old boy presents with chronic fatigue and jaundice. Lab tests reveal nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia and a peripheral smear shows echinocytes. This pathology is likely caused by a deficiency in which glycolytic enzyme?
back:
Pyruvate Kinase (PK).
- Causes insufficient ATP for RBC membrane ion pumps.
- Leads to loss of water and potassium, causing cell deformity.
- Results in premature splenic destruction of erythrocytes.

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: Explain the role of Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate in the metabolic regulation of glycolysis.
back:
- Most potent allosteric activator of PFK-1.
- Overrides inhibition by high ATP levels.
- Levels are increased by insulin and decreased by glucagon.
- Reciprocally inhibits gluconeogenesis by inhibiting Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase.

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: Contrast the kinetic properties and tissue distribution of Hexokinase versus Glucokinase.
back:
- Hexokinase: Found in most tissues; low Km (high affinity); low Vmax; inhibited by G6P.
- Glucokinase: Found in liver and pancreatic beta-cells; high Km (low affinity); high Vmax; not inhibited by G6P.

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: Describe how Pentavalent Arsenic (Arsenate) disrupts the energetics of the glycolytic pathway.
back:
- Competes with inorganic phosphate for Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate Dehydrogenase.
- Produces 3-phosphoglycerate spontaneously without forming 1,3-BPG.
- Bypasses substrate-level phosphorylation.
- Results in zero net ATP yield from glycolysis.

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: Under anaerobic conditions, NADH produced during glycolysis must be reoxidized to NAD+ to allow the pathway to continue; this is catalyzed by the enzyme [___].
back:
Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH).
- Reduces pyruvate to lactate.
- Recycles NAD+ for the Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate Dehydrogenase step.
- Essential for survival in poorly vascularized tissues like the lens.

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: A patient in septic shock exhibits a significant rise in blood lactate levels. Apply your knowledge of glycolysis to explain the metabolic basis of this finding.
back:
- Tissue hypoxia prevents mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.
- Cells rely on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP.
- NADH/NAD+ ratio rises, favoring pyruvate reduction.
- Excess lactate production causes metabolic acidosis.

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: How do mature erythrocytes modify the glycolytic pathway to facilitate oxygen delivery to peripheral tissues during hypoxia?
back:
- Utilize the Rapoport-Luebering Shunt.
- BPG Mutase converts 1,3-BPG to 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate.
- 2,3-BPG binds deoxyhemoglobin and stabilizes the T-state.
- Effectively lowers oxygen affinity, promoting tissue unloading.

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: Contrast the end-products and net energy yield of aerobic versus anaerobic glycolysis per molecule of glucose.
back:
- Aerobic: Produces 2 Pyruvate, 2 ATP, and 2 NADH (yielding more ATP via ETC).
- Anaerobic: Produces 2 Lactate and 2 net ATP only (no net NADH).

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: Identify the primary mechanism through which insulin long-term increases the rate of hepatic glycolysis.
back:
- Induction of gene transcription.
- Increases synthesis of Glucokinase, PFK-1, and Pyruvate Kinase.
- Occurs in response to the well-fed state.
- Increases capacity to process postprandial glucose.

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: The rate-limiting and committed step of glycolysis is the conversion of fructose 6-phosphate to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate, catalyzed by the enzyme [___].
back:
Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1).
* Potently activated by Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate.
* Inhibited by high ATP and Citrate levels.
* Primary regulatory site in glycolysis.

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: A patient presents with garlic-scented breath and severe abdominal pain. In glycolysis, arsenic inhibits the net production of ATP by competing with inorganic phosphate at the [___] enzyme step.
back:
Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH).
* Bypasses substrate-level phosphorylation.
* Forms 1-arseno-3-phosphoglycerate.
* Result: Glycolysis proceeds but produces zero net ATP.

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: Explain the role of the high Km and high Vmax of hepatic glucokinase during the post-prandial state.
back:
* High Km: Low affinity ensures glucose is only captured when portal levels are high.
* High Vmax: Efficiently removes glucose from blood to prevent systemic hyperglycemia.
* Not inhibited by glucose 6-phosphate.

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: Contrast the roles of Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) and Phosphofructokinase-2 (PFK-2) in hepatic glycolytic regulation.
back:
* PFK-1: Rate-limiting enzyme; converts F-6-P to F-1,6-BP.
* PFK-2: Bifunctional enzyme; produces F-2,6-BP (the most potent allosteric activator of PFK-1).
* Glucagon phosphorylates/inactivates PFK-2; Insulin dephosphorylates/activates it.

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: Identify the glycolytic enzyme inhibited by fluoride when collecting blood for glucose estimation and name its required cofactor.
back:
* Enzyme: Enolase.
* Cofactor: Magnesium ($Mg^{2+}$).
* Mechanism: Fluoride forms a complex with phosphate and magnesium, preventing 'in vitro' glycolysis by RBCs.

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: Mature erythrocytes are entirely dependent on glycolysis for energy; a deficiency in [___] is the most common glycolytic cause of non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia.
back:
Pyruvate Kinase (PK).
* Causes decreased ATP yield.
* Leads to failure of Na/K pumps and cell lysis.
* Results in characteristic accumulation of 2,3-BPG.

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: A 50-year-old male in septic shock develops severe metabolic acidosis. Describe the metabolic fate of pyruvate under these hypoxic conditions.
back:
* Reduced to Lactate by Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH).
* Consumes NADH to regenerate NAD+.
* Allows glycolysis to continue in absence of Oxygen.
* Leads to Lactic Acidosis.

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: Identify the two specific reactions in glycolysis that generate ATP via substrate-level phosphorylation.
back:
* 1,3-Bisphosphoglycerate to 3-Phosphoglycerate (Phosphoglycerate Kinase).
* Phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to Pyruvate (Pyruvate Kinase).
* These steps bypass the Electron Transport Chain to produce energy.

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: Distinguish between the significance of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis in terms of end products and ATP yield.
back:
* Aerobic: End product Pyruvate; Net 7 or 8 ATP (via ETC).
* Anaerobic: End product Lactate; Net 2 ATP.
* Anaerobic is vital for RBCs and rapidly contracting muscle.

category: Describe the glycolytic pathway along with its regulation and significance
front: Briefly state the significance of the initial phosphorylation of glucose to glucose 6-phosphate.
back:
* Traps glucose within the cell (G-6-P is polar/charged).
* Maintains concentration gradient for continued glucose entry.
* Commits glucose to intracellular metabolic pathways.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
coreConcept: Role of LDH in anaerobic glycolysis
front: In anaerobic glycolysis, the enzyme [___] is essential for regenerating NAD+ from NADH to allow the glycolytic pathway to continue.
back:
• Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH).
• Reduces pyruvate to lactate.
• Regenerates NAD+ to sustain glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase activity.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: A 24-year-old sprinter experience muscle cramping and fatigue during a 100m dash. This acute state is primarily caused by the accumulation of [___] due to insufficient oxygen supply in the skeletal muscle.
back:
• Lactate (Lactic acid).
• Results from anaerobic glycolysis during intense exercise.
• Causes a drop in intracellular pH, leading to muscle fatigue.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Explain the mechanism by which NADH produced in the cytosol during aerobic glycolysis is utilized to generate ATP.
back:
• Transported into mitochondria via shuttles (Malate-aspartate or Glycerol-3-phosphate).
• Electrons are donated to the Electron Transport Chain (ETC).
• ATP is generated through oxidative phosphorylation.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Contrast the net ATP yield and mitochondrial requirement between aerobic glycolysis and anaerobic glycolysis per glucose molecule.
back:
• Aerobic: Yields 5-7 ATP (including NADH); requires mitochondria for ETC.
• Anaerobic: Yields net 2 ATP; occurs entirely in cytosol without mitochondria.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Identify the primary regulatory enzyme that controls the metabolic flux for both aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis.
back:
• Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1).
• Rate-limiting and committed step.
• Allosterically activated by AMP and Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: The metabolic process in mature erythrocytes is limited to [___] glycolysis because these cells lack mitochondria.
back:
• Anaerobic Glycolysis.
• RBCs lack mitochondria for the TCA cycle and ETC.
• They depend entirely on lactate production for 2 net ATP.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: An infant presents with chronic lactic acidosis and developmental delay. Genetic testing confirms a deficiency in the Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex. How does this deficiency alter glucose metabolism?
back:
• Prevents pyruvate from entering the TCA cycle.
• Forces the cell to rely on anaerobic glycolysis.
• Excess pyruvate is shunted to lactate via LDH.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Describe the fate of the end-product of aerobic glycolysis compared to anaerobic glycolysis in the liver.
back:
• Aerobic: End-product is Pyruvate; converted to Acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle.
• Anaerobic: End-product is Lactate; enters the Cori Cycle for gluconeogenesis.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Distinguish between the Malate-Aspartate and Glycerol 3-Phosphate shuttles regarding energy yield in aerobic glycolysis.
back:
• Malate-Aspartate: Transfers electrons to mitochondrial NAD+; yields ~3 ATP/NADH (total 7 ATP).
• Glycerol 3-Phosphate: Transfers electrons to FAD; yields ~2 ATP/NADH (total 5 ATP).

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: What is the primary significance of the conversion of pyruvate to lactate in anaerobic conditions?
back:
• Regeneration of NAD+.
• Allows the glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase reaction to continue.
• Ensures continued ATP production in the absence of oxygen.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: In the absence of mitochondria or oxygen, the net yield of ATP produced per molecule of glucose during glycolysis is [___].
back: * 2 ATP molecules. * Produced via substrate-level phosphorylation. * No additional ATP is generated during the reduction of pyruvate to lactate.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: A patient in cardiogenic shock develops severe metabolic acidosis. The biochemical explanation involves the regeneration of [___] to allow glycolysis to continue in the absence of oxygen.
back: * NAD+. * Pyruvate is reduced to lactate by Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH). * Reoxidation of NADH is essential to prevent glycolytic arrest at the Glyceraldehyde 3-P stage.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Explain how the presence of oxygen alters the fate of NADH produced during the glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase reaction.
back: * NADH is transported into mitochondria via shuttles. * It is oxidized by the Electron Transport Chain (ETC). * Oxygen acts as the final electron acceptor, yielding ~3 ATP per NADH.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Contrast the energy efficiency and end products of glycolysis in a resting hepatocyte versus an intensely exercising skeletal muscle fiber.
back: * Hepatocyte (Aerobic): Pyruvate end product; ~8 ATP net from glycolysis (2 direct + 6 from 2 NADH). * Exercising Muscle (Anaerobic): Lactate end product; 2 ATP net.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Describe the specific metabolic necessity of the Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) reaction in mature erythrocytes.
back: * RBCs lack mitochondria for oxidative phosphorylation. * LDH reduces pyruvate to lactate to regenerate cytosolic NAD+. * This maintains the Glyceraldehyde 3-P Dehydrogenase step to keep ATP production active.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Under well-oxygenated conditions in cells containing mitochondria, the final three-carbon end product of the glycolytic pathway is [___].
back: * Pyruvate. * It enters the mitochondria for oxidative decarboxylation. * Conversion to Acetyl-CoA is catalyzed by the Pyruvate Dehydrogenase (PDH) complex.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: A victim of house-fire smoke inhalation presents with high serum lactate levels. Explain the shift in glycolytic flux despite the presence of atmospheric oxygen.
back: * Cyanide/CO inhibits Cytochrome Oxidase (Complex IV) in the ETC. * Halts mitochondrial NADH oxidation. * Cell shifts to anaerobic glycolysis for ATP, producing excessive lactate (Lactic Acidosis).

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: How does the Glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle differ from the Malate-aspartate shuttle in terms of net ATP yield during aerobic glycolysis?
back: * Glycerol 3-P Shuttle: NADH is oxidized to FADH2, yielding ~2 ATP. * Malate-aspartate Shuttle: NADH is regenerated as mitochondrial NADH, yielding ~3 ATP.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Distinguish between aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis regarding their cellular location and requirement for molecular oxygen.
back: * Location: Both occur strictly in the cytosol. * Oxygen: Aerobic requires O2 for mitochondrial NADH reoxidation; Anaerobic is oxygen-independent.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: State the net total ATP generated from one molecule of glucose through the complete aerobic pathway (Glycolysis + PDH + TCA).
back: * 36 to 38 ATP molecules. * The variation depends on the specific shuttle used for cytosolic NADH transport. * Significantly higher than the 2 ATP of anaerobic glycolysis.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: In anaerobic glycolysis, the net yield of ATP produced per molecule of glucose is [___].
back:
• 2 ATP.
• Produced via substrate-level phosphorylation.
• NADH is used to reduce pyruvate to lactate, yielding no extra energy.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: A marathon runner experiences muscle fatigue and lactic acid buildup due to local hypoxia. In this anaerobic state, what is the net ATP gain per molecule of glucose consumed?
back:
• 2 ATP.
• Substrate-level phosphorylation occurs at Phosphoglycerate Kinase and Pyruvate Kinase steps.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Explain the role of the energy investment phase in determining the final net ATP yield of glycolysis.
back:
• Consumption of 2 ATP.
• Occurs at Hexokinase and Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) steps.
• Subtracts from the 4 gross ATP produced later, leaving a net of 2.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Contrast the total aerobic ATP yield of glycolysis when using the Malate-aspartate shuttle versus the Glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle.
back:
• Malate-aspartate: ~8 ATP (2 substrate + 6 from 2 NADH).
• Glycerol 3-phosphate: ~6 ATP (2 substrate + 4 from 2 NADH).

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Name the specific enzymes responsible for the substrate-level phosphorylation that generates 4 gross ATP during the energy payoff phase.
back:
• Phosphoglycerate Kinase.
• Pyruvate Kinase.
• Each enzyme produces 1 ATP per triose (2 per glucose).

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: In the absence of oxygen, the total ATP yield remains 2 because the cytosolic [___] cannot be oxidized by the electron transport chain.
back:
• NADH.
• It is instead reoxidized to NAD+ by Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) to keep glycolysis running.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: A mature erythrocyte metabolizes glucose for energy. Given that these cells lack mitochondria, how many net ATP molecules are produced per glucose molecule?
back:
• 2 ATP.
• RBCs are limited to anaerobic glycolysis.
• They lack the machinery for oxidative phosphorylation.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Describe the mechanism by which aerobic glycolysis produces significantly more ATP than anaerobic glycolysis.
back:
• Oxidative Phosphorylation.
• 2 cytosolic NADH enter mitochondria via shuttles.
• Electrons are passed to the ETC, generating 4-6 additional ATP.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Distinguish between the 'Gross ATP' and 'Net ATP' produced during the transition of one glucose molecule to two pyruvate molecules.
back:
• Gross: 4 ATP (Total produced in payoff phase).
• Net: 2 ATP (Gross minus 2 ATP invested in the preparatory phase).

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Calculate the total ATP produced from the aerobic breakdown of glucose solely within the cytosol (excluding the Link Reaction and TCA Cycle).
back:
• 6 to 8 ATP.
• Includes 2 ATP (net substrate-level) and 4-6 ATP (oxidative via NADH shuttles).

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: The continued progression of anaerobic glycolysis in the absence of oxygen depends on the regeneration of [___] via the reduction of pyruvate to lactate.
back:
• NAD+
• Regenerated by Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH)
• Necessary for Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase activity
• Prevents glycolytic arrest during hypoxia

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: An elite sprinter experiences localized muscle pain and a drop in pH during a 100m dash. Identify the metabolic end product responsible and its primary recycling pathway in the liver.
back:
• Product: Lactate
• Pathway: Cori Cycle
• Lactate travels to the liver for gluconeogenesis
• Converts back to glucose for systemic reuse

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Explain the difference in the metabolic fate of NADH when comparing glycolysis in a mature erythrocyte versus a myocardial cell.
back:
• Erythrocyte (Anaerobic): NADH reduces pyruvate to lactate in the cytosol.
• Myocardial Cell (Aerobic): NADH enters mitochondria via shuttles for oxidative phosphorylation in the ETC.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Contrast the net ATP yield and mitochondrial requirement for a single molecule of glucose being oxidized in a septic patient with tissue hypoperfusion versus a healthy individual at rest.
back:
• Septic (Anaerobic): 2 ATP; occurs entirely in the cytosol without oxygen.
• Healthy (Aerobic): 30-32 ATP; requires mitochondria and oxygen for the TCA/ETC.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Specify the primary rate-limiting enzyme for both aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis and its key allosteric inhibitors.
back:
• Enzyme: Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1)
• Inhibitors: ATP and Citrate
• High energy signals (ATP) turn off the pathway to prevent overproduction.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Under normoxic conditions, pyruvate is primarily transported into the mitochondrial matrix and converted into [___] to initiate the Citric Acid Cycle.
back:
• Acetyl CoA
• Catalyzed by Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex
• Represents the commitment to aerobic metabolism
• Irreversible oxidative decarboxylation step

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: A patient with severe anemia exhibits elevated serum lactate levels despite normal atmospheric oxygen levels. Relate this finding to the metabolic limitations of mature Red Blood Cells (RBCs).
back:
• RBCs lack mitochondria
• Rely exclusively on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP
• All pyruvate is converted to lactate even in normoxia
• Energy is required for membrane ion pump maintenance

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Describe the 'Pasteur Effect' and how it influences the rate of glucose consumption in a yeast cell transitioned from anaerobic to aerobic environments.
back:
• Aerobic conditions increase ATP efficiency
• High ATP inhibits PFK-1 (feedback inhibition)
• Glycolytic rate decreases when oxygen is present
• Prevents wasteful rapid glucose consumption

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Distinguish between the two shuttle mechanisms that transfer aerobic glycolytic reducing equivalents into the mitochondrial matrix.
back:
• Malate-Aspartate: Yields ~3 ATP; predominant in heart/liver.
• Glycerol 3-Phosphate: Yields ~2 ATP; predominant in brain/skeletal muscle.
• Shuttles are essential as mitochondria are impermeable to NADH.

category: Compare key features of aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Identify the standard cellular location for the enzymes of glycolysis and the primary reason why it can occur in almost every cell of the human body.
back:
• Location: Cytosol
• Reason: It does not require organelles (mitochondria) or oxygen initially.
• Essential for cells lacking specialized internal structures like RBCs.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: In the energy investment phase of glycolysis, [___] molecules of ATP are consumed to phosphorylate glucose and fructose 6-phosphate.
back:
• Two (2) ATP molecules.
• Consumed by Hexokinase/Glucokinase and Phosphofructokinase-1.
• Required to prime the pathway for the payoff phase.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: A marathon runner experiences muscle cramping and a drop in tissue pH during a final sprint. Identify the net ATP yield per glucose molecule during this anaerobic state.
back:
• 2 ATP (net).
• Pyruvate is converted to lactate to recycle NAD+.
• ATP is generated exclusively through substrate-level phosphorylation.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Explain the role of the Malate-Aspartate shuttle in determining the final ATP yield from glycolytic NADH in aerobic conditions.
back:
• Transfers electrons from cytosolic NADH to mitochondrial NAD+.
• Yields approximately 2.5 (3) ATP per NADH.
• Predominant in heart, liver, and kidney tissues.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Contrast the total ATP yield of aerobic glycolysis in the heart versus skeletal muscle based on the utilized shuttle system.
back:
• Heart/Liver (Malate-Aspartate): ~32 ATP total.
• Skeletal Muscle/Brain (Glycerol-3-P): ~30 ATP total.
• Difference is due to FADH2 versus NADH mitochondrial entry.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Specify the two specific enzymes responsible for substrate-level phosphorylation (ATP production) during the payoff phase of glycolysis.
back:
• Phosphoglycerate Kinase (1,3-BPG to 3-PG).
• Pyruvate Kinase (PEP to Pyruvate).
• Produces a gross total of 4 ATP per glucose.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: The net gain of ATP in anaerobic glycolysis is exactly [___] molecules per glucose, as NADH is reoxidized to NAD+ in the cytosol.
back:
• 2 ATP.
• Gross production is 4 ATP; 2 are consumed.
• Essential for RBCs as they lack mitochondria.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: An infant with hemolytic anemia shows decreased ATP levels in erythrocytes due to Pyruvate Kinase deficiency. State the resulting net ATP yield in these cells.
back:
• Zero (0) net ATP.
• The 2 ATP produced earlier are consumed in the preparatory phase.
• Prevents maintenance of RBC membrane integrity.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Describe how the reduction of pyruvate to lactate prevents the cessation of ATP production in oxygen-starved skeletal muscle.
back:
• Regenerates cytosolic NAD+ from NADH.
• NAD+ is a required co-factor for Glyceraldehyde 3-P Dehydrogenase.
• Allows continued substrate-level phosphorylation without the electron transport chain.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Distinguish between the gross and net ATP production during the conversion of one molecule of glucose to two molecules of pyruvate.
back:
• Gross: 4 ATP produced.
• Net: 2 ATP (4 produced minus 2 consumed).
• Does not include ATP generated from mitochondrial NADH oxidation.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: List the two preparatory phase enzymes that act as the 'ATP-consumers' in the initial steps of glucose metabolism.
back:
• Hexokinase (or Glucokinase in liver).
• Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1).
• Each utilizes one ATP molecule per glucose chain.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: During anaerobic glycolysis of one molecule of glucose, the net gain of energy is [___] molecules of ATP.
back:
* Net yield is 2 ATP.
* 4 ATP are produced via substrate-level phosphorylation.
* 2 ATP are consumed during the priming phase (Hexokinase and PFK-1).

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: A mature erythrocyte, lacking mitochondria, converts one glucose molecule into lactate. Identify the gross number of ATP produced before accounting for energy investment.
back:
* Gross production is 4 ATP.
* Occurs at Phosphoglycerate kinase and Pyruvate kinase steps.
* 2 ATP are produced per triose phosphate molecule.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Explain the mechanism by which 4 ATP are generated in the 'payoff phase' of glycolysis.
back:
* Occurs via substrate-level phosphorylation.
* Phosphoglycerate kinase converts 1,3-BPG to 3-phosphoglycerate (2 ATP per glucose).
* Pyruvate kinase converts Phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to pyruvate (2 ATP per glucose).

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Contrast the theoretical total ATP yield of aerobic glycolysis when using the Malate-aspartate shuttle versus the Glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle.
back:
* Malate-aspartate: ~3 ATP per NADH (Total 6 from 2 NADH).
* Glycerol-3-phosphate: ~2 ATP per NADH (Total 4 from 2 NADH).
* Shuttles transport cytosolic NADH reducing equivalents into mitochondria.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Identify the specific glycolytic reactions that represent the 'investment phase' and the number of ATP consumed.
back:
* 2 ATP consumed total.
* Reaction 1: Hexokinase/Glucokinase (Glucose to Glucose-6-P).
* Reaction 3: Phosphofructokinase-1 (Fructose-6-P to Fructose-1,6-bisP).

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: In anaerobic conditions, the net ATP yield is restricted to 2 because the 2 molecules of NADH produced are utilized by the enzyme [___] to reduce pyruvate.
back:
* Enzyme: Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH).
* Consumes NADH to regenerate NAD+ for continued glycolysis.
* Result: No net ATP from NADH in anaerobic states.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: A patient is exposed to arsenate, which competes with inorganic phosphate at the Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) step. What is the effect on the net ATP yield?
back:
* Net ATP yield becomes zero.
* Arsenate bypasses the 1,3-BPG step.
* The ATP-generating reaction at Phosphoglycerate kinase is skipped.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Describe why the energy yield of aerobic glycolysis is significantly higher than anaerobic glycolysis in terms of NADH fate.
back:
* Aerobic: NADH enters Electron Transport Chain via shuttles, yielding ~4-6 additional ATP.
* Anaerobic: NADH is used to produce lactate, yielding 0 additional ATP.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Distinguish the net ATP yield of one molecule of glucose from the net ATP yield of one molecule of Glyceraldehyde-3-Phosphate (G3P) continuing through the pathway.
back:
* Glucose: Net 2 ATP (4 produced, 2 used).
* G3P: Net 2 ATP (2 produced, 0 used for this specific molecule).
* G3P enters directly into the payoff phase.

category: Calculate the number of ATP produced during aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis
front: Calculate the total theoretical ATP yield of one glucose molecule from the start of glycolysis through the completion of aerobic cytosolic reactions (including ETC).
back:
* Total: 6 to 8 ATP.
* 2 Net ATP from substrate-level phosphorylation.
* 4 or 6 ATP from 2 NADH (depending on the shuttle used).

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: The metabolic process that synthesizes ATP by directly transferring a phosphate group from a high-energy intermediate to ADP, independent of the electron transport chain, is called [___].
back:
* Substrate-level phosphorylation.
* Occurs during glycolysis and the TCA cycle.
* Does not require a mitochondrial proton gradient or oxygen.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: A patient with cyanide poisoning experiences cellular hypoxia because the electron transport chain is inhibited. Despite this, the cell continues to produce a minimal amount of ATP via [___].
back:
* Substrate-level phosphorylation.
* Maintains energy production under anaerobic or toxic conditions.
* Occurs in the cytosol (glycolysis) and mitochondrial matrix (TCA).

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: Explain how the energy derived from the oxidation of NADH and FADH2 is converted into ATP during oxidative phosphorylation.
back:
* Electrons flow through ETC complexes creating a proton gradient.
* Chemiosmotic pressure drives protons back through ATP synthase.
* This rotation catalyzes the phosphorylation of ADP to ATP.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: Contrast the location and energy source of substrate-level phosphorylation versus oxidative phosphorylation in a eukaryotic cell.
back:
* SLP: Found in cytosol/mitochondrial matrix; uses high-energy phosphate bonds.
* OxPhos: Occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane; uses the electrochemical proton gradient.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: Identify the specific reactions in the Tricarboxylic Acid (TCA) cycle and glycolysis where ATP/GTP is generated through substrate-level phosphorylation.
back:
* Glycolysis: Phosphoglycerate kinase and Pyruvate kinase reactions.
* TCA cycle: Succinate thiokinase (Succinyl-CoA synthetase) reaction.
* These are direct energy-capturing steps.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: In oxidative phosphorylation, the enzyme complex that acts as a molecular motor to synthesize ATP using the energy of a dissipated proton gradient is [___].
back:
* ATP Synthase (Complex V).
* Consists of Fo (membrane channel) and F1 (catalytic) domains.
* It couples chemiosmosis to phosphorylation.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: An athlete performing an intense sprint develops lactic acidosis. In the absence of sufficient oxygen for oxidative phosphorylation, the primary mechanism sustaining ATP levels in the myocytes is [___].
back:
* Anaerobic glycolysis via substrate-level phosphorylation.
* Pyruvate is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD+.
* Provides rapid but limited energy without oxygen.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: Describe the role of the 'proton gradient' in the coupling of electron transport to ATP synthesis.
back:
* It acts as the common intermediate storing potential energy.
* Created by pumping H+ from matrix to intermembrane space.
* Dissipation through Complex V powers ATP production.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: Distinguish between the oxygen requirements of substrate-level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation.
back:
* SLP: Anaerobic; occurs directly in the absence of oxygen.
* OxPhos: Aerobic; requires oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor for the ETC.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: Name the specific high-energy thioester intermediate in the TCA cycle that enables substrate-level phosphorylation.
back:
* Succinyl-CoA.
* Its high-energy bond cleavage drives GDP to GTP formation.
* This represents the only SLP step in the mitochondria.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: Pyruvate kinase deficiency leads to hemolytic anemia primarily because mature erythrocytes lack [___], making them entirely dependent on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP production.
back: Mitochondria (Red blood cells cannot utilize oxidative phosphorylation and rely solely on the pyruvate kinase step to generate essential ATP for membrane maintenance.)

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: A 5-year-old boy presents with chronic jaundice, splenomegaly, and echinocytes on peripheral smear. Lab tests reveal low ATP and high 2,3-BPG levels. What is the most likely biochemical defect?
back: Pyruvate Kinase (PK) deficiency (The inability to convert phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate causes ATP depletion and upstream accumulation of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate.)

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: Explain the mechanism by which ATP depletion in pyruvate kinase-deficient red cells leads to splenic sequestration.
back: Low ATP causes Na+/K+ ATPase pump failure, leading to potassium loss and dehydration. This results in rigid, non-deformable cells that are trapped and destroyed by splenic macrophages.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: Contrast the shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve in Pyruvate Kinase (PK) deficiency with that seen in Hexokinase deficiency.
back: PK deficiency: Right shift (increased 2,3-BPG enhances O2 unloading). Hexokinase deficiency: Left shift (decreased 2,3-BPG increases O2 affinity).

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: Identify the metabolic consequence of a glycolytic 'block' at the pyruvate kinase step regarding the intermediate 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate.
back: 1,3-BPG accumulates and is diverted into the Rapoport-Luebering shunt, leading to markedly elevated levels of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG).

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: In the final step of glycolysis, pyruvate kinase catalyzes the conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate, simultaneously generating one molecule of [___] via substrate-level phosphorylation.
back: ATP (Adenosine triphosphate).

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: A patient with pyruvate kinase deficiency remains relatively asymptomatic during exercise despite a low hemoglobin level. Explain the biochemical basis for this exercise tolerance.
back: Elevated 2,3-BPG levels decrease hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, promoting more efficient oxygen delivery to the tissues during periods of high demand.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: Describe how the failure of ATP-dependent ion pumps in PK-deficient erythrocytes specifically causes the formation of 'echinocytes' (burr cells).
back: Intracellular ATP depletion prevents active transport of ions; the resulting loss of intracellular water and potassium causes the cell membrane to shrink and form characteristic spiny projections.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: Distinguish the primary site of red cell destruction in Pyruvate Kinase deficiency from the site of destruction in G6PD deficiency during an acute crisis.
back: PK deficiency: Extravascular hemolysis (spleen/liver). G6PD deficiency: Intravascular and extravascular hemolysis (due to Heinz body damage and oxidative stress).

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: Name the inheritance pattern and the specific clinical classification of the anemia found in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency.
back: Autosomal recessive; Chronic non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: In the final step of anaerobic glycolysis, pyruvate kinase catalyzes the conversion of [___] to pyruvate, generating one molecule of ATP per substrate processed.
back: Phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP)

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: A 5-month-old male presents with jaundice, splenomegaly, and normocytic anemia. The peripheral smear shows spiculated 'echinocytes.' This condition results from a deficiency in an enzyme that produces [___] in erythrocytes.
back:
ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate)
* Deficiency prevents maintenance of Na+/K+ ATPase membrane pumps.
* Leads to cell dehydration, shrinkage, and splenic sequestration.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: Explain why pyruvate kinase deficiency primarily affects mature erythrocytes despite the enzyme being essential in almost all tissues.
back:
* RBCs lack mitochondria and depend solely on anaerobic glycolysis for energy.
* Other tissues utilize oxidative phosphorylation as a backup energy source.
* ATP loss specifically causes RBC membrane collapse.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: Contrast the peripheral smear findings and typical metabolic triggers of Pyruvate Kinase (PK) deficiency with those of G6PD deficiency.
back:
* PK Deficiency: Echinocytes (prickle cells); no drug or food triggers.
* G6PD Deficiency: Heinz bodies and Bite cells; triggered by oxidant stress (Fava beans, drugs).

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: Identify the specific glycolytic intermediate that acts as a potent allosteric 'feed-forward' activator of hepatic pyruvate kinase.
back:
* Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate.
* It ensures the rate of the final step matches the activity of PFK-1.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: In Pyruvate Kinase deficiency, the chronic accumulation of upstream glycolytic intermediates leads to an increased concentration of [___], which shifts the oxygen-dissociation curve.
back: 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG)

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: A patient with PK deficiency shows a lower-than-expected level of physical fatigue despite significant anemia. Explain the biochemical compensation responsible for this finding.
back:
Elevated 2,3-BPG levels.
* High 2,3-BPG decreases hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen.
* Enhances oxygen unloading at peripheral tissues to compensate for low hemoglobin.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: Describe the biochemical sequence from low ATP production to the formation of spiculated echinocytes in PK-deficient red blood cells.
back:
* ATP-dependent Na+/K+ pumps fail.
* Intracellular K+ and water exit the cell.
* Cell dehydration leads to shrinkage and characteristic membrane spiculations.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: Contrast the hormonal regulation of pyruvate kinase in the liver versus its regulation in skeletal muscle during the fasting state.
back:
* Liver: Glucagon induces cAMP-mediated phosphorylation and inactivation.
* Muscle: Not affected by glucagon; primarily regulated by local energy demands (ATP/AMP).

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: What is the end product of pyruvate metabolism in a normal mature erythrocyte, and which enzyme is essential for regenerating NAD+ for glycolysis?
back:
* End product: Lactate.
* Enzyme: Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH).
* Required to maintain NAD+ levels for glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: In glycolysis, the enzyme [___] catalyzes the direct transfer of a high-energy phosphate group from phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to ADP, representing a classic example of substrate-level phosphorylation.
back:
* **Pyruvate Kinase**
* Directly synthesizes ATP without an electron transport chain
* Represents the final irreversible step of glycolysis
* Occurs solely in the cytosol.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: A patient with severe hypoxia continues to produce ATP despite an inactive Electron Transport Chain. This survival mechanism is solely reliant on [___].
back:
* **Substrate-level phosphorylation**
* Energy is derived directly from metabolic intermediates
* Functions independently of oxygen levels
* Facilitated primarily through anaerobic glycolysis.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: Explain the fundamental mechanism by which oxidative phosphorylation couples electron transport to ATP synthesis according to the chemiosmotic theory.
back:
* **Proton Pumping**: ETC complexes pump H+ into the intermembrane space
* **Proton Gradient**: Creates an electrochemical potential across the inner membrane
* **ATP Synthase**: H+ flow back through Complex V drives ATP formation.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: Contrast the source of energy used for phosphate attachment in substrate-level phosphorylation versus oxidative phosphorylation.
back:
* **SLP**: Energy comes from high-energy phosphate bonds within the substrate (e.g., 1,3-BPG)
* **OXPHOS**: Energy comes from the electrochemical proton-motive force generated by redox reactions in the ETC.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: Identify the two specific cellular locations within a hepatocyte where substrate-level phosphorylation occurs.
back:
* **Cytosol**: During Glycolysis (Phosphoglycerate Kinase and Pyruvate Kinase steps)
* **Mitochondrial Matrix**: During the TCA cycle (Succinate Thiokinase step converting Succinyl-CoA to Succinate).

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: The membrane-bound enzyme complex responsible for the final physical step of oxidative phosphorylation by utilizing a proton gradient is [___].
back:
* **ATP Synthase (Complex V)**
* Spans the inner mitochondrial membrane
* Consists of F0 (pore) and F1 (catalytic) domains
* Dissipates the pH and electrical gradients to phosphorylate ADP.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: A patient accidentally ingests 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP). While the ETC continues rapidly, ATP synthesis drops because DNP disrupts [___].
back:
* **Oxidative Phosphorylation**
* DNP acts as an **uncoupler**
* It makes the inner mitochondrial membrane permeable to H+
* The proton gradient is dissipated as heat instead of driving ATP Synthase.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: Detail why substrate-level phosphorylation is the only source of ATP in mature erythrocytes.
back:
* **Lack of Mitochondria**: Erythrocytes cannot perform the TCA cycle or OXPHOS
* **Anaerobic Glycolysis**: They rely entirely on cytosolic SLP
* **Metabolic End**: Pyruvate is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD+.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: Distinguish between the final electron acceptors in substrate-level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation.
back:
* **SLP**: Uses organic metabolic intermediates (no external acceptor needed)
* **OXPHOS**: Requires **Molecular Oxygen (O2)** as the terminal electron acceptor to form water.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: Name the specific high-energy intermediate produced in the TCA cycle that facilitates substrate-level phosphorylation.
back:
* **Succinyl-CoA**
* Cleaved by **Succinate Thiokinase**
* Provides energy to phosphorylate GDP to GTP (or ADP to ATP)
* Occurs in the mitochondrial matrix.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: Pyruvate kinase catalyzes the irreversible final step of glycolysis, converting phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to [___], which generates the ATP necessary for erythrocyte membrane integrity.
back: Pyruvate. - This reaction provides the second substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis. - In RBCs, this is the primary source of metabolic energy.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: A neonate presents with jaundice and non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia. Lab findings reveal significantly elevated 2,3-BPG levels and low erythrocyte ATP. What is the underlying biochemical diagnosis?
back: Pyruvate Kinase (PK) Deficiency. - It is the second most common cause of enzyme-deficiency hemolytic anemia. - Most common cause of the Embden-Meyerhof pathway defects.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: Describe the biochemical consequence of ATP depletion on the erythrocyte membrane in Pyruvate Kinase deficiency.
back: Failure of Na+/K+ ATPase pumps leads to: - Intracellular potassium loss and water efflux. - Cellular dehydration and formation of 'echinocytes' (spiculated cells). - Increased membrane rigidity and splenic destruction.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: Contrast the compensatory oxygen-unloading mechanism in Pyruvate Kinase (PK) deficiency with that of Hexokinase (HK) deficiency.
back: PK Deficiency: Elevated 2,3-BPG shifts the O2-dissociation curve to the right, aiding tissue unloading. - HK Deficiency: Decreased 2,3-BPG shifts the curve to the left, hindering tissue oxygenation.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: Why does Pyruvate Kinase deficiency cause hemolysis specifically in RBCs while sparing tissues like the liver or muscle?
back: Mature RBCs lack mitochondria and depend entirely on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP. - Liver and muscle cells utilize oxidative phosphorylation, providing alternative energy sources to bypass the PK block.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: The characteristic spiculated appearance of red blood cells seen on a peripheral smear in pyruvate kinase deficiency is primarily caused by [___].
back: Cellular Dehydration. - Caused by electrolyte imbalance from Na+/K+ pump failure. - These cells are often termed 'echinocytes' or 'burr cells'.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: A child with chronic anemia and splenomegaly has a lower-than-normal hemoglobin affinity for oxygen (Right Shift). Explain the biochemical basis for this finding.
back: Obstruction of the PK step causes upstream accumulation of 1,3-BPG. - This is shunted to 2,3-BPG via the Rapoport-Luebering cycle. - 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxyhemoglobin, facilitating oxygen release to tissues.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: Explain the role of the reticuloendothelial system in the pathogenesis of anemia in Pyruvate Kinase deficiency.
back: The spleen acts as a biological filter. - Dehydrated, rigid echinocytes cannot deform to pass through splenic sinusoids. - They are sequestered and destroyed by splenic macrophages (extravascular hemolysis).

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: Distinguish between the triggers for hemolysis in G6PD deficiency versus Pyruvate Kinase (PK) deficiency.
back: G6PD Deficiency: Episodic hemolysis triggered by oxidative stress (drugs, fava beans, infection). - PK Deficiency: Continuous, chronic non-spherocytic hemolysis due to a constitutive metabolic defect.

category: Explain hemolytic anemia in subjects with pyruvate kinase deficiency based on your biochemical knowledge
front: What is the primary mode of inheritance for Pyruvate Kinase deficiency commonly encountered in clinical practice?
back: Autosomal Recessive. - Most affected individuals are compound heterozygotes. - Consanguinity is a frequent risk factor in UHS board scenarios.

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: In the glycolytic pathway, ATP is generated via [___], a process that occurs directly in the cytosol without the use of the electron transport chain or a proton gradient.
back:
* Substrate-level phosphorylation (SLP)
* Direct phosphate transfer from a high-energy intermediate to ADP
* Does not require oxygen or mitochondria

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
coreConcept: Compensatory ATP Production in Toxic Hypoxia
front: A patient presents with sudden collapse after cyanide exposure, which inhibits Cytochrome c oxidase. While oxidative phosphorylation is halted, the cell continues to produce minimal ATP through [___].
back:
* Substrate-level phosphorylation
* Provides anaerobic ATP source
* Occurs in Glycolysis (cytosol) and TCA cycle (matrix)
* Insufficient for high-energy organs (brain/heart)

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: Explain the fundamental mechanism by which oxidative phosphorylation couples electron transport to ATP synthesis according to the Mitchell hypothesis.
back:
* ETC pumps protons into intermembrane space
* Creates an electrochemical/pH gradient
* Protons flow back through Complex V (ATP Synthase)
* Chemiosmotic energy drives phosphorylation of ADP

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: Contrast the immediate source of energy used for phosphate attachment in substrate-level phosphorylation versus oxidative phosphorylation.
back:
* SLP: Energy from high-energy chemical bonds (thioesters/phosphates)
* OXPHOS: Energy from the proton-motive force (electrochemical gradient)
* SLP is a direct chemical reaction; OXPHOS is indirect

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: Identify the specific reaction within the mitochondrial matrix that produces a high-energy phosphate (GTP/ATP) strictly via substrate-level phosphorylation.
back:
* Conversion of Succinyl-CoA to Succinate
* Enzyme: Succinate thiokinase (Succinyl-CoA synthetase)
* High-energy thioester bond cleavage drives phosphorylation
* Part of the TCA cycle

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: While oxidative phosphorylation yields approximately [___] ATP per molecule of NADH, substrate-level phosphorylation always yields exactly one ATP/GTP per reacting molecule.
back:
* 3 (or 2.5) ATP
* OXPHOS yield depends on proton pumping efficiency
* SLP yield is stoichiometric and fixed

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and cannot perform oxidative phosphorylation. To maintain the Na+/K+ ATPase pump, they rely exclusively on ATP generated by [___].
back:
* Substrate-level phosphorylation
* Occurs during Glycolysis
* Key enzymes: Phosphoglycerate kinase and Pyruvate kinase
* Vital for maintaining RBC shape and membrane integrity

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: Describe the necessity of molecular oxygen in oxidative phosphorylation compared to its role in substrate-level phosphorylation.
back:
* OXPHOS: O2 is the final electron acceptor; without it, ETC stalls
* SLP: Oxygen is not required (anaerobic)
* OXPHOS is the primary aerobic energy source

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: Differentiate between the types of enzymes that catalyze substrate-level phosphorylation versus those that finalize oxidative phosphorylation.
back:
* SLP: Soluble kinases (e.g., Pyruvate kinase) in cytosol/matrix
* OXPHOS: Membrane-bound ATP Synthase (Complex V)
* SLP uses direct chemical transfer; OXPHOS utilizes a physical proton channel

category: Clearly differentiate between substrate level phosphorylation and oxidative phosphorylation
front: Name the two specific glycolytic intermediates that serve as high-energy phosphate donors for substrate-level phosphorylation.
back:
* 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (1,3-BPG)
* Phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP)
* Catalyzed by Phosphoglycerate kinase and Pyruvate kinase respectively

category: Discuss the metabolic fates of pyruvate
front: In aerobic conditions, the irreversible conversion of pyruvate to Acetyl-CoA within the mitochondria is catalyzed by the [___] complex.
back: • Pyruvate Dehydrogenase (PDH) Complex. • Requires 5 coenzymes: TPP, Lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, and NAD+. • Serves as the critical link between glycolysis and the TCA cycle.

category: Discuss the metabolic fates of pyruvate
front: A 55-year-old patient in septic shock presents with severe metabolic acidosis. The biochemical cause is the reduction of pyruvate to [___] to regenerate NAD+.
back: • Lactate. • Catalyzed by Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH). • Essential for maintaining anaerobic glycolysis during tissue hypoxia. • High serum levels indicate poor tissue perfusion.

category: Discuss the metabolic fates of pyruvate
front: Explain the role of the Pyruvate Carboxylase reaction in maintaining metabolic homeostasis during fasting.
back: • Converts pyruvate into Oxaloacetate (OAA). • Requires Biotin (B7) and ATP; activated by Acetyl-CoA. • Essential for replenishing TCA cycle intermediates (anaplerosis) and initiating gluconeogenesis in the liver.

category: Discuss the metabolic fates of pyruvate
front: Contrast the metabolic fates of pyruvate in skeletal muscle during vigorous exercise versus the recovery phase regarding the Glucose-Alanine cycle.
back: • Vigorous Exercise: Pyruvate is transaminated to Alanine (via ALT) to transport nitrogen to the liver. • Recovery: Liver converts Alanine back to pyruvate for gluconeogenesis to replenish blood glucose.

category: Discuss the metabolic fates of pyruvate
front: Identify the specific coenzyme requirement and product of pyruvate decarboxylation in yeast and certain microorganisms.
back: • Product: Ethanol (via Acetaldehyde). • Coenzyme: Thiamine Pyrophosphate (TPP). • Enzyme: Pyruvate Decarboxylase (not found in humans).

category: Discuss the metabolic fates of pyruvate
front: In the initial step of gluconeogenesis, pyruvate is converted to oxaloacetate by the enzyme pyruvate carboxylase, which requires the vitamin-derived cofactor [___].
back:
• Biotin (Vitamin B7).
• Functions as a carrier of activated CO2.
• Catalyzes the ATP-dependent carboxylation reaction.

category: Discuss the metabolic fates of pyruvate
front: A 1-month-old infant presents with developmental delay, muscle spasticity, and severe lactic acidosis. A metabolic block in the conversion of pyruvate to [___] is most likely.
back:
• Acetyl CoA.
• Indicates Pyruvate Dehydrogenase (PDH) complex deficiency.
• Results in pyruvate shunting to lactate via LDH.

category: Discuss the metabolic fates of pyruvate
