• Pentosuria: Deficiency of Xylitol Dehydrogenase; asymptomatic/benign; excretes L-Xylulose.
• Diabetes: Hyperglycemia exceeds renal threshold; associated with metabolic distress; excretes Glucose.
• Diagnosis: Both show positive Benedict's, but Pentosuria is Glucose-Oxidase negative.

category: Describe the reactions, regulation, and biomedical importance of uronic acid pathway and sorbitol pathway
front: Identify the specific metabolic reason why humans cannot synthesize Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid) via the uronic acid pathway.
back:
• Absence of L-gulonolactone oxidase.
• Prevents the conversion of L-gulonate to Ascorbate.
• Makes Vitamin C an essential dietary nutrient for humans and primates.

category: Describe the reactions, regulation, and biomedical importance of uronic acid pathway and sorbitol pathway
front: The reduction of glucose to sorbitol is catalyzed by aldose reductase and requires [___] as a reducing equivalent.
back:
• NADPH.
• Sourced primarily from the Pentose Phosphate Pathway.
• Its depletion in hyperglycemia compromises antioxidant defenses (Reduced Glutathione).

category: Describe the reactions, regulation, and biomedical importance of uronic acid pathway and sorbitol pathway
front: A patient's urine is positive for a reducing sugar by Benedict’s test but negative for the Glucose Oxidase strip test. The patient has no symptoms of diabetes. Name the likely enzyme defect.
back:
• L-Xylulose Reductase (Xylitol Dehydrogenase).
• Condition: Essential Pentosuria.
• High-yield fact: It is a harmless autosomal recessive metabolic anomaly.

category: Describe the reactions, regulation, and biomedical importance of uronic acid pathway and sorbitol pathway
front: Describe the mechanism by which the sorbitol pathway contributes to oxidative stress in chronic hyperglycemia.
back:
• NADPH Depletion: Diverts NADPH from glutathione reductase to aldose reductase.
• Reduced Glutathione (GSH): Levels fall, making the cell vulnerable to H2O2 damage.
• Glycation: High sorbitol/fructose levels increase non-enzymatic glycation of proteins.

category: Describe the reactions, regulation, and biomedical importance of uronic acid pathway and sorbitol pathway
front: Distinguish between the entry points of the Uronic Acid pathway and the Sorbitol pathway from Glycolysis.
back:
• Uronic Acid Pathway: Enters via Glucose-6-Phosphate (converted to Glucose-1-P).
• Sorbitol Pathway: Enters directly from free Glucose.
• Both bypass the ATP-producing steps of Glycolysis.

category: Describe the reactions, regulation, and biomedical importance of uronic acid pathway and sorbitol pathway
front: Identify the end product of the uronic acid pathway that allows it to feed back into the Pentose Phosphate Pathway (PPP).
back:
• D-Xylulose 5-Phosphate.
• Formed via L-Xylulose and Xylitol intermediates.
• Connects uronic acid metabolism to the non-oxidative phase of the PPP.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: In the primary cytosolic reaction of ethanol metabolism, ethanol is oxidized to acetaldehyde by the enzyme [___].
back:
• Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH).
• Requires NAD+ as a cofactor.
• Occurs primarily in the liver cytosol.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: A chronic alcoholic presents with fasting hypoglycemia after heavy drinking. The underlying biochemical cause is an overproduction of [___], which inhibits gluconeogenic pathways.
back:
• NADH (High NADH/NAD+ ratio).
• Shifts pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate.
• Depletes necessary substrates for gluconeogenesis.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Explain how the excessive generation of NADH during ethanol oxidation leads to the development of hepatic steatosis (fatty liver).
back:
• High NADH inhibits the TCA cycle and Fatty Acid oxidation.
• Increases glycerol-3-phosphate levels (from DHAP).
• Stimulates Triacylglycerol (TAG) synthesis and VLDL secretion.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Contrast the kinetics and cellular location of the Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH) pathway with the Microsomal Ethanol Oxidizing System (MEOS).
back:
• ADH: Cytosolic; low Km (high affinity); active at low ethanol levels.
• MEOS: Smooth ER (CYP2E1); high Km; induced in chronic alcoholism or high intake.
• MEOS requires NADPH; ADH requires NAD+.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Identify the mitochondrial enzyme that converts acetaldehyde to acetate and is specifically inhibited by the drug Disulfiram.
back:
• Aldehyde Dehydrogenase (ALDH).
• Inhibition causes acetaldehyde accumulation.
• Leads to nausea, flushing, and tachycardia.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: The metabolic acidosis observed in heavy ethanol consumption is primarily due to the shift of the Pyruvate/Lactate equilibrium toward [___].
back:
• Lactate.
• Driven by a high NADH/NAD+ ratio.
• Results in lactic acidosis and hyperuricemia.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: A patient presents with extreme flushing and headache after taking Metronidazole followed by alcohol. This 'Disulfiram-like' reaction occurs due to the inhibition of [___].
back:
• Aldehyde Dehydrogenase (ALDH).
• Prevents the conversion of toxic acetaldehyde to acetate.
• Common with Metronidazole and some Cephalosporins.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Describe the metabolic fate of Acetate produced in the liver after ethanol ingestion.
back:
• Liver acetate is released into blood.
• Peripheral tissues (e.g., muscle) convert it to Acetyl CoA.
• Catalyzed by Acetyl-CoA synthetase for entry into the TCA cycle.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Distinguish between the roles of NAD+ and NADPH in the overall process of ethanol metabolism in the liver.
back:
• NAD+: Required as an electron acceptor by ADH and ALDH (primary pathways).
• NADPH: Required as an electron donor by the MEOS/CYP2E1 pathway.
• MEOS activation depletes NADPH needed for glutathione reduction.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Name the high-energy molecule synthesized in peripheral tissues from ethanol-derived acetate that allows it to be used as a fuel source.
back:
• Acetyl-CoA.
• Synthesized by Acetyl-CoA synthetase.
• Enters the Citric Acid (TCA) cycle for ATP production.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: The initial step of ethanol metabolism occurs primarily in the cytosol of hepatocytes, where the enzyme [___] converts ethanol into acetaldehyde.
back:
• Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH)
• Requires NAD+ as a coenzyme
• Follows zero-order kinetics
• Produces NADH

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: A patient taking metronidazole experiences severe flushing, nausea, and tachycardia after consuming a small amount of alcohol. This reaction occurs due to the inhibition of [___].
back:
• Aldehyde Dehydrogenase (ALDH)
• Causes acetaldehyde accumulation
• Mechanism identical to Disulfiram therapy
• Blocks mitochondrial ALDH2 isozyme

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Explain the role of the Microsomal Ethanol Oxidizing System (MEOS) in chronic heavy alcohol consumption.
back:
• Uses CYP2E1 in endoplasmic reticulum
• High Km for ethanol
• Induced by chronic drinking
• Requires NADPH and O2

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Contrast the metabolic effects of Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH) and Aldehyde Dehydrogenase (ALDH) regarding coenzyme utilization.
back:
• Both require NAD+ reduction to NADH
• Significantly increases NADH:NAD+ ratio
• Ratio shift inhibits gluconeogenesis
• Favors lactate and fatty acid synthesis

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Identify the metabolic consequence of the excess NADH produced during ethanol oxidation on the pyruvate-lactate equilibrium.
back:
• Shifts equilibrium toward Lactate
• Causes high-anion gap lactic acidosis
• Reduces pyruvate availability for gluconeogenesis
• Explains fasting hypoglycemia in alcoholics

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: The final product of hepatic ethanol metabolism that enters the peripheral tissues to be converted into Acetyl-CoA is [___].
back:
• Acetate
• Produced by ALDH
• Activated by Acetyl-CoA synthetase
• Primarily metabolized in skeletal muscle

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: A 45-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with hepatomegaly. Biopsy shows fatty change (steatosis). This is caused by the high NADH:NAD+ ratio inhibiting [___].
back:
• Fatty acid β-oxidation
• Impairs TCA cycle activity
• Stimulates triacylglycerol synthesis
• Decreases VLDL secretion efficiency

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Describe the biochemical mechanism behind the use of Fomepizole in methanol poisoning.
back:
• Competitive inhibitor of ADH
• Prevents conversion to formaldehyde
• Blocks production of toxic formic acid
• High affinity for ADH enzyme

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Contrast the genetic variations of Aldehyde Dehydrogenase (ALDH2) common in East Asian populations with the standard variant.
back:
• ALDH2*2 has much higher Km
• Results in low acetaldehyde affinity
• Causes rapid alcohol-flush reaction
• Protective against alcoholism

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Specify the subcellular location for the conversion of acetaldehyde to acetate during alcohol metabolism.
back:
• Mitochondria (primary)
• Mediated by ALDH2
• Cytosolic ALDH1 plays minor role
• Acetate then enters systemic circulation

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: The primary cytosolic enzyme responsible for the first step of ethanol metabolism, converting it into acetaldehyde, is [___].
back:
Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH). 
- Requires NAD+ as a coenzyme. 
- Reduces NAD+ to NADH.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: A chronic alcoholic develops fasting hypoglycemia after a drinking binge. This occurs because the high [NADH]/[NAD+] ratio in the liver diverts [___] into lactate, inhibiting its availability for gluconeogenesis.
back:
Pyruvate. 
- High NADH favors the Lactate Dehydrogenase reaction towards lactate. 
- Depletes gluconeogenic precursors. 
- Also inhibits OAA formation from malate.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Explain the role of the Microsomal Ethanol Oxidizing System (MEOS) in chronic drinkers.
back:
Uses cytochrome P450 (CYP2E1). 
- Located in smooth endoplasmic reticulum. 
- Requires NADPH and O2. 
- Highly induced by chronic ethanol consumption, increasing tolerance.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Contrast the metabolic consequences of ethanol oxidation via the primary ADH pathway versus the MEOS pathway.
back:
ADH Pathway: Primary source; produces NADH; localized in cytosol/mitochondria. 
- MEOS: Minor source; consumes NADPH; localized in SER. 
- MEOS induction increases oxidative stress and drug metabolism interactions.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Identify the mitochondrial enzyme that converts acetaldehyde into acetate and its significance in therapy.
back:
Aldehyde Dehydrogenase (ALDH). 
- Target of the drug Disulfiram (Antabuse). 
- Inhibition leads to acetaldehyde accumulation, causing flushing and nausea.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: The highly reactive and toxic intermediate of ethanol metabolism that causes tissue damage and protein adduct formation is [___].
back:
Acetaldehyde. 
- Causes the acute symptoms of hangover. 
- Promotes liver cirrhosis and lipid peroxidation. 
- Oxidized to acetate in mitochondria.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: A patient presents with 'fatty liver' after years of alcohol abuse. Describe the biochemical basis for increased triacylglycerol synthesis in this patient.
back:
High NADH:NAD+ ratio. 
- Inhibits Fatty Acid β-oxidation. 
- Increases Glycerol-3-Phosphate availability. 
- Shifts metabolism towards fatty acid and TG synthesis.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Beyond ADH and MEOS, describe the third minor pathway of ethanol oxidation found in peroxisomes.
back:
Catalase Pathway. 
- Uses Hydrogen Peroxide (H2O2) as an oxidant. 
- Converts ethanol to acetaldehyde. 
- Plays a negligible role in healthy hepatic metabolism.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Distinguish the end-products of the two-step oxidative metabolism of ethanol and their ultimate fate.
back:
Step 1: Acetaldehyde (Toxic intermediate). 
- Step 2: Acetate (Non-toxic end-product). 
- Fate: Acetate is converted to Acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle or fatty acid synthesis.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: State the necessary cofactors for the primary two-step hepatic oxidation of ethanol to acetate.
back:
NAD+ (Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide). 
- Required for both ADH and ALDH enzymes. 
- Pathway produces 2 molecules of NADH per ethanol molecule.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: The primary cytosolic enzyme responsible for the initial step of ethanol metabolism, converting ethanol to acetaldehyde, is [___].
back:
• Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH)
• Requires NAD+ as a cofactor
• Produces NADH and Acetaldehyde
• Primarily located in the liver.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: A chronic alcoholic presents with profound fasting hypoglycemia. Explain the biochemical mechanism involving the NAD+/NADH ratio that inhibits gluconeogenesis in this patient.
back:
• High NADH/NAD+ ratio favors Pyruvate → Lactate
• Shifts Oxaloacetate → Malate
• Depletes gluconeogenic precursors
• Prevents glucose synthesis from non-carbohydrate sources.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Describe the intracellular localization and function of the enzyme Acetaldehyde Dehydrogenase (ALDH) in the ethanol oxidation pathway.
back:
• Mitochondrial localization
• Converts Acetaldehyde to Acetate
• Uses NAD+ as an electron acceptor
• Acetate then enters blood to become Acetyl-CoA.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Contrast the Microsomal Ethanol Oxidizing System (MEOS) with the Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH) pathway regarding cofactor use and induction.
back:
• MEOS: Uses NADPH and O2 (CYP2E1); induced by high ethanol levels.
• ADH: Uses NAD+; constitutive (not induced).
• MEOS consumes energy; ADH yields energy (NADH).

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Identify the specific metabolic product of ethanol metabolism that is directly responsible for hepatic steatosis (fatty liver) by inhibiting beta-oxidation.
back:
• Excess NADH
• Inhibits Fatty Acid Oxidation
• Promotes Triacylglycerol synthesis
• Leads to VLDL accumulation and fatty deposits.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: The accumulation of [___] is the primary cause of toxic effects such as nausea, flushing, and tachycardia during alcohol consumption.
back:
• Acetaldehyde
• Highly reactive and toxic intermediate
• Usually rapidly converted by ALDH
• High levels occur with ALDH deficiency or inhibition.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: A patient is treated with Disulfiram for alcohol dependence. If they consume alcohol, they experience severe illness. What is the molecular target of this drug?
back:
• Irreversible inhibition of ALDH
• Causes massive acetaldehyde buildup
• Triggers 'disulfiram-like reaction'
• Prevents conversion of acetaldehyde to acetate.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Explain the biochemical link between ethanol ingestion and the development of hyperuricemia and gouty flares in susceptible patients.
back:
• Lactic acidosis (from high NADH) competes with Urate for renal excretion
• Ethanol metabolism increases ATP breakdown
• Leads to increased purine degradation
• Results in elevated serum Uric Acid.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Distinguish between the fate of the Acetate produced in the liver from ethanol and its subsequent utilization in peripheral tissues.
back:
• Liver: Acetate is released into the blood.
• Peripheral Tissues: Converted to Acetyl-CoA by Acetyl-CoA synthetase.
• Enters TCA cycle for energy production.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: State the standard caloric value provided by the metabolic oxidation of one gram of ethanol in the human body.
back:
• 7 kcal/g
• Intermediate between carbohydrates (4 kcal/g) and fats (9 kcal/g)
• Provides 'empty calories' lacking micronutrients.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: The metabolism of ethanol by alcohol dehydrogenase and acetaldehyde dehydrogenase significantly increases the cytosolic [___] ratio, leading to metabolic derangements.
back:
• NADH/NAD+
• This shift is the primary driver of alcohol-induced hypoglycemia and steatosis.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: A chronic alcoholic presents with tremors and a blood glucose of 40 mg/dL. The inhibition of which metabolic process is primarily responsible for this hypoglycemia?
back:
• Gluconeogenesis inhibition
• Sequestration of precursors (Pyruvate and OAA)
• Driven by the high NADH/NAD+ ratio shifting equilibria away from glucose synthesis.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Explain why pyruvate cannot be effectively utilized for glucose synthesis during active ethanol consumption.
back:
• High NADH favors the reduction of Pyruvate to Lactate
• Catalyzed by Lactate Dehydrogenase
• Depletes Pyruvate availability for the Pyruvate Carboxylase reaction.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Contrast the effect of ethanol-induced high NADH levels on Dihydroxyacetone Phosphate (DHAP) in glycolysis versus its contribution to fatty liver.
back:
• Glycolysis: DHAP is diverted away from Glyceraldehyde-3-P
• Fatty Liver: DHAP is reduced to Glycerol-3-phosphate
• Provides the glycerol backbone for increased Triglyceride synthesis.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Describe the effect of chronic ethanol ingestion on the Mitochondrial ̢-oxidation of fatty acids.
back:
• Inhibition of ̢-oxidation
• High NADH signals an energy-rich state to the mitochondria
• Accumulated fatty acids are re-esterified into triglycerides, causing steatosis.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: The accumulation of triglycerides within hepatocytes due to altered metabolic flux in alcoholism is termed hepatic [___].
back:
• Steatosis (or Fatty Liver)
• Results from increased synthesis and decreased oxidation of fatty acids.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: A patient after an ethanol binge shows elevated serum lactate and malate. Relate these specific findings to the risk of fasting hypoglycemia.
back:
• High NADH/NAD+ ratio shifts Pyruvate to Lactate
• Shifts Oxaloacetate to Malate
• Both processes deplete the substrates required for the gluconeogenic pathway.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Detail how ethanol-mediated changes in the NAD+ pool affect the Citric Acid Cycle (TCA) and contribute to liver fat accumulation.
back:
• NADH inhibits Isocitrate Dehydrogenase and ̑-Ketoglutarate Dehydrogenase
• TCA cycle slows significantly
• Acetyl-CoA is diverted from oxidation to Fatty Acid synthesis.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Distinguish between the fate of Acetyl-CoA in a healthy fasting state versus a fasting state during ethanol metabolism.
back:
• Healthy Fasting: Enters TCA cycle for ATP production
• Ethanol Metabolism: TCA cycle is inhibited; Acetyl-CoA is used for lipogenesis and ketogenesis.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Identify the two sequential enzymes in the liver responsible for generating high levels of NADH during ethanol clearance.
back:
• Alcohol Dehydrogenase (Ethanol to Acetaldehyde)
• Acetaldehyde Dehydrogenase (Acetaldehyde to Acetate)
• Both steps require NAD+ as a cofactor.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: The metabolism of ethanol by alcohol dehydrogenase and acetaldehyde dehydrogenase leads to a significant increase in the hepatic [___] ratio.
back:
• NADH:NAD+ ratio.
• This shift drives many reversible reactions toward their reduced products.
• It is the fundamental cause of ethanol-induced metabolic disturbances.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: A chronic alcoholic presents with severe fasting hypoglycemia after a 24-hour binge. What is the primary biochemical mechanism preventing gluconeogenesis in this patient?
back:
• High NADH/NAD+ ratio.
• Pyruvate is diverted to Lactate by LDH.
• Oxaloacetate is diverted to Malate.
• This depletes essential gluconeogenic precursors.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Explain the role of Dihydroxyacetone Phosphate (DHAP) in the development of ethanol-induced fatty liver.
back:
• High NADH/NAD+ ratio drives DHAP reduction to Glycerol-3-phosphate.
• Glycerol-3-phosphate provides the backbone for TAG synthesis.
• Increased availability promotes fatty acid esterification into TAGs.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Contrast the metabolic fates of Pyruvate and Oxaloacetate in the liver during acute ethanol intoxication.
back:
• Pyruvate: Reduced to Lactate, contributing to lactic acidosis.
• Oxaloacetate: Reduced to Malate, inhibiting PEP-carboxykinase entry.
• Both diversions block glucose synthesis from non-carbohydrate sources.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Why is mitochondrial fatty acid β-oxidation inhibited during ethanol consumption?
back:
• β-oxidation requires NAD+ as an electron acceptor.
• Ethanol metabolism saturates the liver with NADH.
• The resulting NAD+ deficiency halts the breakdown of fatty acids.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: The end product of ethanol metabolism, [___], is activated to Acetyl-CoA, which directly serves as a substrate for hepatic lipogenesis.
back:
• Acetate.
• It is activated by acetyl-CoA synthetase.
• Provides the building blocks for excessive fatty acid synthesis.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: A heavy drinker is found to have a blood pH of 7.25 and elevated lactate. Identify the specific enzymatic reaction responsible for this lactate accumulation.
back:
• Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH).
• High NADH drives the reaction: Pyruvate + NADH + H+ → Lactate + NAD+.
• Results in lactic acidosis and hyperlactatemia.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Describe the mechanism by which ethanol-induced NADH accumulation affects the Malate-Aspartate shuttle and its clinical significance.
back:
• Favors the conversion of Oxaloacetate to Malate.
• Malate is trapped in the mitochondria or exported unnecessarily.
• Depletes cytosolic Oxaloacetate needed for gluconeogenesis.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Distinguish between the effect of ethanol on hepatic fatty acid synthesis versus fatty acid oxidation.
back:
• Synthesis: Increased due to high Acetyl-CoA and Glycerol-3-P.
• Oxidation: Decreased due to lack of NAD+.
• Net effect: Accumulation of TAGs in hepatocytes (Steatosis).

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Identify the primary cytosolic enzyme that initiates ethanol metabolism in hepatocytes and its required coenzyme.
back:
• Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH).
• Requires NAD+ (which is reduced to NADH).
• Located primarily in the cytosol of hepatocytes.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
coreConcept: Hepatic Redox State Shift in Ethanol Metabolism
front: The primary biochemical disturbance in hepatocytes following significant ethanol ingestion is a marked increase in the [___] ratio.
back: The **NADH/NAD+ ratio**. Excess NADH is generated by the sequential actions of alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase, shifting the cell's redox state.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: A chronic alcoholic found unconscious after a 48-hour fast presents with severe hypoglycemia. Inhibition of which metabolic pathway is responsible for this clinical emergency?
back: The **Gluconeogenesis** pathway. High NADH levels deplete essential precursors (pyruvate and oxaloacetate), preventing the liver from synthesizing glucose once glycogen stores are exhausted.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Explain the mechanism by which ethanol consumption promotes the synthesis of the glycerol backbone needed for triacylglycerol accumulation (fatty liver).
back: Excessive NADH drives the **Glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase** reaction to convert dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) into **glycerol 3-phosphate**, providing the backbone for fat synthesis.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Contrast the effect of high NADH levels on fatty acid metabolism versus the TCA cycle during ethanol oxidation.
back: High NADH inhibits **$\beta$-oxidation** of fatty acids and slows the **TCA cycle** (inhibiting isocitrate dehydrogenase), resulting in Acetyl-CoA being shunted toward fatty acid synthesis.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: State the specific fate of Pyruvate in the presence of the high NADH/NAD+ ratio produced by heavy drinking.
back: Pyruvate is reduced to **Lactate** by Lactate Dehydrogenase to regenerate NAD+. This causes lactic acidosis and prevents pyruvate from entering gluconeogenesis.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Ethanol metabolism inhibits the conversion of Malate back to [___], effectively blocking the entry of carbon skeletons into the gluconeogenic pathway.
back: **Oxaloacetate (OAA)**. The high NADH/NAD+ ratio favors the reduction of OAA to Malate, depleting the substrate required for PEP-carboxykinase.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: A patient presents with a 'fatty liver' on ultrasound after years of alcohol abuse. Which lipoprotein's inability to match increased hepatic TAG synthesis leads to this condition?
back: **VLDL (Very-Low-Density Lipoprotein)**. When the rate of triacylglycerol synthesis exceeds the liver's capacity to export them as VLDL, steatosis (fatty liver) occurs.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Describe the link between ethanol-induced ketoacidosis and the inhibition of the TCA cycle.
back: High NADH/NAD+ inhibits the TCA cycle, causing **Acetyl-CoA** to accumulate. This excess Acetyl-CoA is diverted into the ketogenesis pathway, producing acetoacetate and $\beta$-hydroxybutyrate.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Distinguish between the subcellular locations of the two primary enzymes of ethanol metabolism and the cofactors they utilize.
back: Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH) is **cytosolic**; Aldehyde Dehydrogenase (ALDH) is **mitochondrial**. Both enzymes require **NAD+** as a cofactor and produce NADH.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Identify the three gluconeogenic intermediates that are 'drained' by the high NADH/NAD+ ratio, leading to hypoglycemia.
back:
1. **Pyruvate** (drained to Lactate)
2. **Oxaloacetate** (drained to Malate)
3. **DHAP** (drained to Glycerol 3-P)

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: The primary cytosolic enzyme responsible for the conversion of ethanol to acetaldehyde, using NAD+ as a cofactor, is [___].
back:
Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH)
*   Reduces NAD+ to NADH.
*   Follows zero-order kinetics.
*   Found primarily in the liver.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: A patient taking Metronidazole for an infection experiences severe flushing, tachycardia, and vomiting after consuming a single alcoholic beverage. Identify the metabolic intermediate that has accumulated.
back:
Acetaldehyde
*   Metronidazole inhibits **Acetaldehyde Dehydrogenase (ALDH)**.
*   Produces a toxic 'disulfiram-like reaction'.
*   Aldehyde accumulation causes systemic vasodilation and nausea.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Explain the metabolic mechanism by which acute ethanol intoxication leads to fasting hypoglycemia.
back:
NADH-induced substrate depletion
*   High **NADH:NAD+ ratio** shifts pyruvate to lactate.
*   Shifts oxaloacetate to malate.
*   Depletes key substrates required for gluconeogenesis.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Contrast the Ethanol oxidation via the Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH) pathway with the Microsomal Ethanol Oxidizing System (MEOS).
back:
ADH vs. MEOS
*   **ADH:** Cytosolic, low Km (high affinity), NAD+ dependent.
*   **MEOS:** Microsomal (ER), high Km (low affinity), NADPH dependent; induced by chronic heavy drinking (CYP2E1).

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Describe the specific kinetic model followed by Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH) at social drinking concentrations.
back:
Zero-Order Kinetics
*   Metabolized at a constant rate regardless of blood concentration.
*   Enzyme is saturated even at low alcohol levels.
*   Average clearance is ~7–10g/hour.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: The mitochondrial enzyme Acetaldehyde Dehydrogenase (ALDH) converts acetaldehyde into [___], which can then be utilized as Acetyl-CoA.
back:
Acetate
*   The final product of hepatic ethanol metabolism.
*   Most acetate enters systemic circulation.
*   Converted to Acetyl-CoA in peripheral tissues by Acetyl-CoA synthetase.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: A chronic alcoholic presents with hepatomegaly; biopsy reveals macrovesicular steatosis. Relate the NADH:NAD+ ratio to this finding.
back:
Fatty Liver (Steatosis)
*   High NADH inhibits **β-oxidation** of fatty acids.
*   Excess NADH promotes **glycerol-3-phosphate** production.
*   Favors triacylglycerol synthesis and accumulation in hepatocytes.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: How does the induction of the MEOS pathway in chronic alcoholics increase the risk of Acetaminophen (Paracetamol) toxicity?
back:
CYP2E1 Induction
*   Chronic ethanol induces **CYP2E1**.
*   Accelerates conversion of acetaminophen to the toxic metabolite **NAPQI**.
*   Depletes glutathione, leading to acute hepatic necrosis.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Distinguish between the cellular locations of the first and second oxidative steps of ethanol metabolism.
back:
Location of Oxidation
*   **Step 1 (ADH):** Occurs in the **Cytosol**.
*   **Step 2 (ALDH):** Occurs in the **Mitochondrial matrix**.

category: Outline the reactions involved in ethanol metabolism
front: Summarize the direct effect of ethanol ingestion on gastric acid secretion based on biochemical GIT principles.
back:
HCl Stimulation
*   Acts as a direct stimulant of gastric glands.
*   Triggers **Gastrin** release from G-cells.
*   Resulting gastric juice is rich in HCl and pepsin.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Ethanol metabolism in the hepatocyte by alcohol dehydrogenase significantly increases the intracellular [___] ratio, which is the root cause of metabolic derangements like hypoglycemia.
back:
• NADH/NAD+ ratio
• High NADH inhibits gluconeogenic enzymes
• Shifts metabolic equilibria toward reduced products
• Prevents the liver from maintaining blood glucose levels.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
coreConcept: Lactic Acidosis and Hypoglycemia in Alcoholics
front: A 40-year-old chronic alcoholic is found unresponsive after a 24-hour fast. Laboratory studies show severe hypoglycemia and elevated serum lactate. What biochemical shift involving pyruvate explains this finding?
back:
• High NADH/NAD+ ratio
• Pyruvate is reduced to Lactate to regenerate NAD+
• Pyruvate is diverted away from gluconeogenesis
• Results in substrate depletion for glucose synthesis.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Explain the role of Dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) in the development of ethanol-induced fatty liver (steatosis).
back:
• High NADH drives DHAP reduction to Glycerol 3-phosphate
• Glycerol 3-phosphate provides the backbone for triglycerides
• Leads to increased triacylglycerol synthesis
• Results in lipid accumulation (fatty liver).

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Contrast the metabolic fate of Oxaloacetate (OAA) during a normal fast versus a fast complicated by ethanol consumption.
back:
• Normal Fast: OAA enters gluconeogenesis via PEP-carboxykinase
• Ethanol Fast: High NADH reduces OAA to Malate
• OAA is unavailable for glucose synthesis
• Direct cause of ethanol-induced fasting hypoglycemia.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Identify the primary enzyme and coenzyme used in the first step of ethanol oxidation in the liver cytosol.
back:
• Enzyme: Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH)
• Coenzyme: NAD+
• Function: Converts Ethanol to Acetaldehyde
• Side Effect: Produces NADH, altering the cell's redox state.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: The inhibition of [___] is the primary reason fatty acids cannot be utilized for energy during ethanol metabolism, contributing to fatty liver.
back:
• Beta-oxidation (Fatty acid oxidation)
• High NADH levels inhibit the pathway enzymes
• Fatty acids are diverted into triglyceride synthesis
• Promotes hepatocyte lipid droplets (steatosis).

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: A patient with long-term ethanol dependence presents with hepatomegaly and a 'greasy' liver on biopsy. How does the slowdown of the Citric Acid Cycle (TCA) contribute to this condition?
back:
• High NADH inhibits Isocitrate Dehydrogenase
• Acetyl-CoA accumulates due to stalled TCA cycle
• Excess Acetyl-CoA is used for Fatty Acid Synthesis
• Synergistic effect with inhibited beta-oxidation.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Describe the mechanism by which the 'redox state' change from ethanol metabolism prevents the conversion of lactate back to glucose.
back:
• High NADH/NAD+ ratio inhibits Lactate Dehydrogenase (forward)
• Favors the conversion of Pyruvate → Lactate
• Prevents the conversion of Lactate → Pyruvate
• Blocks the entry of lactate into gluconeogenesis.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Contrast the effects of NADH accumulation on Acetyl-CoA fate during ethanol consumption versus the well-fed state.
back:
• Well-fed: Acetyl-CoA is primarily for energy or stored as fat via insulin
• Ethanol: Stalled TCA cycle forces Acetyl-CoA into lipogenesis
• NADH inhibits oxidation and promotes synthesis
• Leads to pathological fatty liver even in fasting.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Name the two specific organelles where the two-step oxidation of ethanol into acetate occurs in hepatocytes.
back:
• Cytosol: Ethanol → Acetaldehyde (via ADH)
• Mitochondria: Acetaldehyde → Acetate (via ALDH)
• Both steps generate NADH
• Acetate can later enter the Acetyl-CoA pool.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Chronic ethanol consumption leads to a high intracellular [___] ratio, which is the primary metabolic driver for inhibited gluconeogenesis and increased lipogenesis.
back:
• NADH/NAD+ ratio.
• High NADH shifts hepatic metabolism away from glucose production.
• Promotes fatty acid synthesis and lactic acid production.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: A 45-year-old chronic alcoholic is found unresponsive after a 2-day binge without food. Laboratory tests reveal blood glucose of 40 mg/dL and elevated serum lactate. Identify the mechanism shifting pyruvate away from gluconeogenesis.
back:
• High NADH/NAD+ ratio drives Pyruvate to Lactate.
• Depletes pyruvate needed for glucose synthesis.
• Causes fasting hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Explain the biochemical basis of fatty liver (steatosis) in the context of altered hepatic NADH levels following ethanol ingestion.
back:
• NADH inhibits mitochondrial β-oxidation of fatty acids.
• High NADH promotes DHAP conversion to Glycerol-3-phosphate.
• Accelerates triacylglycerol synthesis and VLDL accumulation in hepatocytes.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Contrast the fate of Oxaloacetate in the liver of a healthy fasting person versus an individual with acute ethanol toxicity.
back:
• Normal: Oxaloacetate is utilized for gluconeogenesis.
• Ethanol: High NADH reduces Oxaloacetate to Malate.
• Depletion of Oxaloacetate directly halts the glucose-producing pathway.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Discuss the impact of increased NADH on the Citric Acid Cycle (TCA) during acute ethanol intoxication.
back:
• High NADH inhibits Isocitrate Dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate Dehydrogenase.
• Acetyl-CoA is diverted from the TCA cycle toward ketone body synthesis.
• Results in alcoholic ketoacidosis.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: The accumulation of [___] in the liver during ethanol metabolism causes significant oxidative stress and is responsible for protein adduct formation and tissue damage.
back:
• Acetaldehyde.
• Reactive intermediate produced by Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH).
• Promotes inflammation, lipid peroxidation, and cellular injury.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: A patient presents with painful muscle cramps and high serum uric acid levels after heavy alcohol use. Relate the NADH-induced shift in pyruvate metabolism to this secondary hyperuricemia.
back:
• Ethanol metabolism causes lactic acidosis.
• Lactate competes with Urate for renal tubule excretion.
• Decreased urate clearance leads to hyperuricemia and gout exacerbation.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Delineate the biochemical link between ethanol metabolism and the overproduction of VLDL leading to hepatic steatosis.
back:
• Excess NADH inhibits FA oxidation and stimulates lipogenesis.
• High Glycerol-3-Phosphate increases TAG assembly.
• TAGs are packaged into VLDL; excess VLDL leads to lipid droplets.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Distinguish between the roles of Alcohol Dehydrogenase (ADH) and the Microsomal Ethanol Oxidizing System (MEOS) regarding NAD+/NADPH usage.
back:
• ADH: Low Km; produces NADH in the cytosol/mitochondria.
• MEOS (CYP2E1): High Km; induced in chronic use; consumes NADPH.
• MEOS contributes to oxidative stress and drug interactions.

category: Explain how ethanol consumption causes hypoglycemia and fatty liver
front: Name the two specific enzymes that generate the high hepatic NADH/NAD+ ratio during ethanol catabolism.
back:
• Alcohol Dehydrogenase (Ethanol to Acetaldehyde).
• Acetaldehyde Dehydrogenase (Acetaldehyde to Acetate).
• Both reactions reduce NAD+ to NADH.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: The terminal electron carrier in the respiratory chain that reacts directly with molecular oxygen to form water is [___].
back: - Cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV). - Contains copper ions (Cu-A and Cu-B). - Final step in electron transfer to O2.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: A patient accidentally ingests the pesticide Rotenone. Which specific protein complex in the inner mitochondrial membrane is inhibited, and what happens to the oxidation of NADH?
back: - Inhibits Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase). - Blocks electron transfer to Coenzyme Q. - NADH remains in the reduced state; ATP synthesis stops.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Describe the sequential flow of electrons starting from FADH2 produced in the TCA cycle.
back: - Complex II (Succinate dehydrogenase). - Coenzyme Q (Ubiquinone). - Complex III (Cytochrome bc1 complex). - Cytochrome c. - Complex IV (Cytochrome oxidase). - Molecular Oxygen (final acceptor).

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Contrast the proton-pumping capabilities of Complex I and Complex II during electron transport.
back: - Complex I: Pumps protons into the intermembrane space (contributes to gradient). - Complex II: Does not pump protons. - Complex II lacks sufficient free energy release for pumping.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Identify the mobile electron carriers that bridge the large, fixed protein complexes in the mitochondrial membrane.
back: - Coenzyme Q (Ubiquinone): Hydrophobic lipid-soluble carrier between Complexes I/II and III. - Cytochrome c: Water-soluble peripheral protein between Complexes III and IV.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: The only enzyme of the Citric Acid Cycle that is physically embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane as part of the ETC is [___].
back: - Succinate Dehydrogenase (Complex II). - Transfers electrons from Succinate to FAD. - Directly links the TCA cycle and ETC.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: A victim of structural fire presents with cherry-red skin and cellular hypoxia despite high oxygen saturation. What specific site in the ETC is blocked by the suspected toxin?
back: - Carbon Monoxide or Cyanide poisoning. - Blocks Cytochrome a+a3 (Complex IV). - Inhibits the final reduction of O2 to H2O.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Explain how the Glycerophosphate shuttle bypasses Complex I to transport cytosolic reducing equivalents into the mitochondrial ETC.
back: - Cytosolic NADH reduces DHAP to Glycerol-3-P. - Mitochondrial Glycerol-3-P dehydrogenase reduces FAD to FADH2. - FADH2 transfers electrons directly to Coenzyme Q, bypassing Complex I.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
coreConcept: P:O Ratios of NADH and FADH2
front: Distinguish between the oxidation of NADH and FADH2 regarding their total ATP yield via the ETC.
back: - NADH: Yields ~3 ATP (enters at Complex I, 3 pumping sites). - FADH2: Yields ~2 ATP (enters at Complex II, only 2 pumping sites). - ATP yield is proportional to protons pumped.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Delineate the precise anatomical location of the Electron Transport Chain within the mitochondrion.
back: - Inner Mitochondrial Membrane. - Specifically organized into folds called cristae. - Impermeable to most ions to maintain the proton gradient.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: The first protein complex of the electron transport chain, NADH dehydrogenase, contains a tightly bound prosthetic group called [___] that accepts two hydrogen atoms from NADH.
back:
* **Flavin mononucleotide (FMN)**
* It accepts 2 electrons and 2 protons from NADH.
* It becomes FMNH2 and initiates the transfer of electrons to iron-sulfur (Fe-S) centers.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: A technician in a chemical plant is found unconscious with a bitter almond odor on his breath. Lab results show severe lactic acidosis. This toxin inhibits the electron transport chain by binding to [___].
back:
* **Cytochrome a+a3 (Complex IV)**
* Cyanide binds to the ferric (Fe3+) iron of the heme group.
* This arrests the reduction of oxygen to water, stopping ATP synthesis.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Describe the unique organizational position and function of Cytochrome c within the respiratory chain.
back:
* **Location:** Associated with the outer face of the inner mitochondrial membrane.
* **Function:** Acts as a mobile electron carrier.
* **Transfer:** Shuttles electrons from Complex III (Cytochrome bc1) to Complex IV (Cytochrome oxidase).

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Contrast the entry points of electrons into the ETC derived from NADH versus those derived from Succinate.
back:
* **NADH:** Enters via Complex I (NADH Dehydrogenase); pumps 4 protons across the membrane.
* **Succinate:** Enters via Complex II (Succinate Dehydrogenase); uses FAD and does not pump protons.
* **Convergence:** Both pathways donate electrons to Coenzyme Q.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Identify the only non-protein component of the electron transport chain and its structural adaptation for function.
back:
* **Coenzyme Q (Ubiquinone)**
* **Structure:** A lipophilic quinone derivative with a long, hydrophobic isoprenoid tail.
* **Role:** A mobile carrier that moves through the lipid bilayer from Complexes I and II to III.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: In the mitochondrial respiratory chain, the final electron acceptor that combines with protons to form water is [___].
back:
* **Molecular Oxygen (O2)**
* It occurs at Complex IV (Cytochrome oxidase).
* Oxygen is reduced to H2O using four electrons and four protons.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: A child presents with hyperpyrexia (fever) and rapid breathing after accidentally ingesting a large bottle of aspirin. The underlying biochemical mechanism involves the [___] of oxidative phosphorylation.
back:
* **Uncoupling**
* High-dose salicylates increase inner membrane permeability to protons.
* The proton gradient dissipates as heat instead of being captured as ATP, causing hyperthermia.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Explain the role and valence changes of Iron-Sulfur (Fe-S) centers during the transfer of electrons through Complex I and III.
back:
* **Role:** Serve as electron transfer agents within the protein complexes.
* **Valence Changes:** The iron atoms oscillate between the ferric (Fe3+) and ferrous (Fe2+) states.
* **Transfer:** They carry one electron at a time.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Distinguish between the effects of Oligomycin and 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP) on the mitochondrial proton gradient.
back:
* **Oligomycin:** Blocks the Fo channel of ATP synthase; stops proton flow into matrix; increases the gradient.
* **DNP:** Acts as a protonophore; carries protons across the membrane; dissipates the gradient as heat.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Specify the structural feature of the inner mitochondrial membrane that maximizes the capacity for electron transport assemblies.
back:
* **Cristae (highly convoluted folds)**
* They greatly increase the surface area of the inner membrane.
* This allows for a higher density of ETC complexes and ATP synthase units per mitochondrion.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: The protein complexes of the electron transport chain (ETC) are embedded within the [___] of the mitochondrion.
back:
Inner Mitochondrial Membrane
- Specifically concentrated in the cristae
- Provides a large surface area for oxidative phosphorylation
- Highly impermeable to ions.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: A victim of house-fire smoke inhalation presents with cherry-red skin and metabolic acidosis. The toxin involved inhibits the ETC by binding to the heme iron of [___].
back:
Cytochrome a + a3 (Complex IV)
- Toxin: Carbon Monoxide (CO) or Cyanide (CN-)
- Blocks the final transfer of electrons to oxygen
- Halts the respiratory chain and ATP production.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Explain why Coenzyme Q (Ubiquinone) is uniquely capable of transferring electrons from both Complex I and Complex II to Complex III.
back:
- It is a non-protein, lipophilic mobile carrier
- Contains a long isoprenoid tail allowing diffusion within the lipid bilayer
- Links flavoproteins to the cytochrome series.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Contrast the redox components of Complex I with those of Complex II in terms of their respective initial electron donors.
back:
- Complex I (NADH Dehydrogenase): Receives electrons from NADH; contains FMN and Fe-S centers.
- Complex II (Succinate Dehydrogenase): Receives electrons from FADH2; contains FAD and Fe-S centers.
- Complex II does not pump protons.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Identify the metabolic consequence of electrons entering the ETC via FADH2 instead of NADH regarding the proton gradient.
back:
- Lower ATP yield (P:O ratio approx 2:1 vs 3:1)
- Electrons bypass the proton pump at Complex I
- Fewer total protons are pumped into the intermembrane space.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: The only member of the respiratory chain that can react directly with molecular oxygen is [___].
back:
Cytochrome oxidase (Complex IV / Cyto a+a3)
- Contains copper atoms (CuA and CuB)
- Reduces O2 to two molecules of water
- Final step of electron flow.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: An athlete takes a synthetic compound that increases the permeability of the inner mitochondrial membrane to protons. Predict the effect on the ETC rate and ATP synthesis.
back:
- ETC rate: Increases (loss of respiratory control)
- ATP synthesis: Decreases (uncoupling)
- Energy is dissipated as heat (e.g., 2,4-Dinitrophenol).

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Detail the path of an electron starting from the oxidation of Succinate until it reaches Cytochrome C.
back:
1. Succinate → FADH2 (Complex II)
2. Complex II → Coenzyme Q (Ubiquinone)
3. Coenzyme Q → Complex III (Cytochrome bc1)
4. Complex III → Cytochrome C.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Distinguish between the localization of Cytochrome C and the other cytochrome complexes within the mitochondrion.
back:
- Cytochrome C: Peripheral membrane protein located on the outer face of the inner membrane (intermembrane space).
- Complexes I, III, IV: Integral proteins spanning the inner membrane.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Name the non-heme iron-containing structures that act as prosthetic groups to facilitate single-electron transfers within Complexes I, II, and III.
back:
Iron-Sulfur (Fe-S) Centers
- Also known as non-heme iron proteins
- Exist in several forms (e.g., 2Fe-2S, 4Fe-4S)
- Mediate transfer between flavins and cytochromes.

category: Enlist various types of glycogen storage diseases (GSDs)
coreConcept: Enzymatic Defect in Von Gierke Disease
front: Glycogen Storage Disease Type I (Von Gierke's) is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme [___], leading to severe fasting hypoglycemia.
back:
• Glucose-6-phosphatase
• Impairs the final step of both gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis
• Presents with hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, and hyperuricemia

category: Enlist various types of glycogen storage diseases (GSDs)
front: A 4-month-old infant presents with massive cardiomegaly, hypotonia, and early heart failure. Biopsy shows glycogen accumulation in lysosomes. What is the diagnosis?
back:
• Pompe Disease (GSD Type II)
• Deficiency: Lysosomal acid alpha-1,4-glucosidase (acid maltase)
• Only GSD that is also categorized as a Lysosomal Storage Disease

category: Enlist various types of glycogen storage diseases (GSDs)
front: Explain why GSD Type III (Cori's disease) results in the accumulation of glycogen with shorter-than-normal outer branches.
back:
• Deficiency: Debranching enzyme (alpha-1,6-glucosidase)
• Phosphorylase acts until four residues remain (limit dextrin)
• Absence of debrancher stops further breakdown, leaving short outer chains

category: Enlist various types of glycogen storage diseases (GSDs)
front: Contrast the abnormal glycogen structure in Andersen Disease (GSD IV) versus Cori Disease (GSD III).
back:
• Andersen (IV): Long, unbranched chains (amylopectin-like) due to Branching Enzyme deficiency
• Cori (III): Short, highly branched outer chains (limit dextrins) due to Debranching Enzyme deficiency

category: Enlist various types of glycogen storage diseases (GSDs)
front: Identify the key laboratory finding regarding blood lactate levels in McArdle Disease following strenuous ischemic exercise.
back:
• Failure of blood lactate levels to rise
• Normal rise in blood ammonia levels
• Due to deficiency of Myophosphorylase (GSD Type V)

category: Enlist various types of glycogen storage diseases (GSDs)
front: The enzyme deficient in GSD Type IV (Andersen's), which typically leads to early liver cirrhosis and infantile death, is [___].
back:
• Branching enzyme (Amylo-alpha-1,4→1,6-transglucosidase)
• Responsible for creating alpha-1,6 glycosidic bonds
• Deficiency causes accumulation of insoluble, toxic polysaccharides

category: Enlist various types of glycogen storage diseases (GSDs)
front: A 25-year-old presents with muscle cramps and wine-colored urine after intense exercise. Muscle biopsy shows glycogen accumulation. Name the likely condition.
back:
• McArdle Disease (GSD Type V)
• Wine-colored urine indicates myoglobinuria
• Caused by deficiency in skeletal muscle glycogen phosphorylase

category: Enlist various types of glycogen storage diseases (GSDs)
front: Describe the mechanism by which Von Gierke's disease (GSD I) results in secondary hyperuricemia and gout.
back:
• Accumulation of Glucose-6-phosphate increases flux through the Pentose Phosphate Pathway
• Leads to excess Ribose-5-phosphate production
• Results in increased purine synthesis and subsequent degradation to uric acid

category: Enlist various types of glycogen storage diseases (GSDs)
front: Distinguish between Von Gierke (GSD I) and Hers Disease (GSD VI) regarding the severity of fasting hypoglycemia.
back:
• Von Gierke (I): Severe (impairs both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis)
• Hers (VI): Mild (only glycogenolysis is impaired; gluconeogenesis remains intact)

category: Enlist various types of glycogen storage diseases (GSDs)
front: List the specific GSD types that primarily involve hepatic enzymes and present with hepatomegaly and fasting hypoglycemia.
back:
• Type I (Von Gierke)
• Type III (Cori)
• Type VI (Hers)
• Type IX (Phosphorylase kinase deficiency)

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: In the mitochondrial respiratory chain, the mobile lipid-soluble quinone that shuttles electrons from Complexes I and II to Complex III is [___].
back: • Ubiquinone (Coenzyme Q) • Transports electrons through the lipid bilayer • Links flavoproteins to cytochromes • Can carry one or two electrons (semiquinone)

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: A child presents with hypotonia and developmental delay. Biopsy reveals a deficiency in the protein complex that accepts hydride ions from NADH. Identify the complex and its prosthetic groups.
back: • Complex I (NADH Dehydrogenase) • Transfers electrons from NADH to CoQ • Contains Flavin Mononucleotide (FMN) • Utilizes multiple Iron-Sulfur (Fe-S) centers

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Describe the sequence of electron flow through the Electron Transport Chain starting specifically from FADH2 generated in the TCA cycle.
back: • Electrons enter at Complex II (Succinate Dehydrogenase) • Pass to Ubiquinone (CoQ) • Flow to Complex III, then Cytochrome c • Final transfer to Complex IV to reduce Oxygen

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Contrast the specific inhibition site of Rotenone with that of Antimycin A regarding the flow of electrons in the respiratory chain.
back: • Rotenone: Inhibits transfer from Fe-S centers of Complex I to CoQ • Antimycin A: Inhibits transfer from Cytochrome b to c1 in Complex III • Antimycin A blocks both NADH and FADH2 flow

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Identify the metallic centers within Complex IV (Cytochrome c oxidase) that are essential for the final reduction of molecular oxygen.
back: • Heme a and Heme a3 • Copper centers (CuA and CuB) • Binds O2 at the a3-CuB binuclear center • Reduces O2 to two molecules of H2O

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: The mitochondrial enzyme that oxidizes Succinate to Fumarate while transferring electrons directly to the Electron Transport Chain is [___].
back: • Complex II (Succinate Dehydrogenase) • Only ETC complex that is also a TCA cycle enzyme • Does not pump protons across the membrane • Uses FAD as a cofactor

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: A patient presenting with a 'bitter almond' breath odor after chemical exposure exhibits a complete block of oxygen consumption. This toxin targets which specific component of the ETC?
back: • Cyanide (or Carbon Monoxide) • Binds to the Ferric (Fe3+) iron in Cytochrome a3 • Occurs within Complex IV • Halts ATP synthesis and causes rapid cell death

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Explain how Cytochrome c functions differently from Coenzyme Q (Ubiquinone) as a mobile carrier within the mitochondrial membrane.
back: • Cytochrome c: Water-soluble protein on the intermembrane space side • Shuttles single electrons between Complexes III and IV • CoQ: Lipid-soluble quinone within the membrane bilayer • Shuttles electron pairs between Complexes I/II and III

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Distinguish between the total number of protons pumped into the intermembrane space by electrons entering via NADH versus those entering via Succinate.
back: • NADH path: 10 protons (4 from I, 4 from III, 2 from IV) • Succinate/FADH2 path: 6 protons (4 from III, 2 from IV) • Succinate path bypasses Complex I

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Identify the four major classes of prosthetic groups that facilitate the movement of electrons through the respiratory chain complexes.
back: • Flavins (FMN, FAD) • Cytochromes (Heme iron) • Iron-Sulfur (Fe-S) centers • Copper atoms (CuA, CuB)

category: Infer the key biochemical and clinical features of various GSDs from the respective enzyme deficiencies
front: GSD Type I, also known as Von Gierke disease, is characterized by severe fasting hypoglycemia due to a deficiency in the enzyme [___].
back:
- Glucose-6-phosphatase.
- Essential for final step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
- Leads to hepatomegaly and lactic acidosis.

category: Infer the key biochemical and clinical features of various GSDs from the respective enzyme deficiencies
front: A 4-month-old infant presents with cardiomegaly, macroglossia, and severe hypotonia. Blood glucose levels are normal, but muscle biopsy shows glycogen accumulation in vacuoles. Identify the deficient enzyme.
back:
- Lysosomal α-1,4-glucosidase (Acid Maltase).
- Diagnosis: Pompe Disease (GSD Type II).
- Unique as it is a lysosomal storage disease.

category: Infer the key biochemical and clinical features of various GSDs from the respective enzyme deficiencies
front: Explain why a deficiency in Debranching Enzyme (GSD Type III/Cori Disease) results in the accumulation of abnormally structured glycogen.
back:
- Phosphorylase acts until four residues remain from a branch.
- Absence of 4:4 transferase or 1:6 glucosidase halts further degradation.
- Results in short-branched limit dextrins.

category: Infer the key biochemical and clinical features of various GSDs from the respective enzyme deficiencies
coreConcept: GSD IV vs. GSD VI Differentiation
front: Contrast the hepatic effects of Branching Enzyme deficiency (GSD Type IV) with Liver Phosphorylase deficiency (GSD Type VI).
back:
- GSD IV (Andersen): Long, unbranched glycogen chains; leads to fatal liver cirrhosis.
- GSD VI (Hers): Normal glycogen structure; results in mild hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly.

category: Infer the key biochemical and clinical features of various GSDs from the respective enzyme deficiencies
front: Identify the metabolic rationale for hyperuricemia seen specifically in Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency.
back:
- Accumulated Glucose-6-phosphate shunts to Pentose Phosphate Pathway.
- Increases Ribose-5-phosphate, driving purine synthesis.
- Excess purine degradation leads to uric acid overproduction.

category: Infer the key biochemical and clinical features of various GSDs from the respective enzyme deficiencies
front: In GSD Type V, the enzyme [___] is deficient, preventing the breakdown of glycogen during strenuous muscle contraction.
back:
- Myophosphorylase (Skeletal Muscle Phosphorylase).
- Diagnosis: McArdle Disease.
- Leads to exercise-induced cramps and myoglobinuria.

category: Infer the key biochemical and clinical features of various GSDs from the respective enzyme deficiencies
front: An 18-year-old athlete experiences muscle cramps and burgundy-colored urine after exercise. He notes a 'second wind' phenomenon after resting. Which biochemical finding is expected during a forearm ischemic exercise test?
back:
- Failure of blood lactate to rise.
- Normal blood glucose.
- Myoglobinuria due to rhabdomyolysis.

category: Infer the key biochemical and clinical features of various GSDs from the respective enzyme deficiencies
front: A patient presents with exercise intolerance similar to McArdle disease but also exhibits compensated hemolytic anemia. Describe the likely enzyme defect.
back:
- Muscle Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1).
- Diagnosis: Tarui Disease (GSD Type VII).
- Blocks distal glycolysis; RBCs also affected.

category: Infer the key biochemical and clinical features of various GSDs from the respective enzyme deficiencies
front: Distinguish the metabolic outcomes of Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency from those of Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency regarding glycogen stores.
back:
- GSD I (G6Pase): Excessive liver glycogen accumulation.
- F1,6-BPase Deficiency: Normal glycogen stores, but impaired gluconeogenesis.
- Both cause fasting hypoglycemia.

category: Infer the key biochemical and clinical features of various GSDs from the respective enzyme deficiencies
front: Name the primary glycogen storage organ that remains unaffected in a patient diagnosed with McArdle Disease.
back:
- Liver.
- Liver phosphorylase is a different isozyme.
- Blood glucose regulation remains normal in GSD V.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: The primary enzyme complex in the inner mitochondrial membrane that accepts a hydride ion from NADH and contains a flavin mononucleotide (FMN) coenzyme is [___].
back:
Complex I (NADH Dehydrogenase).
• Transfers electrons to Coenzyme Q (Ubiquinone).
• Couples electron flow to proton pumping.
• Contains iron-sulfur centers for electron relay.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: A patient exposed to house-fire smoke presents with cherry-red skin and cellular hypoxia. This clinical state results from the binding of carbon monoxide to the heme iron of [___].
back:
Complex IV (Cytochrome a + a3).
• Also known as Cytochrome c oxidase.
• Blocks the final transfer of electrons to oxygen.
• Arrests ATP production via oxidative phosphorylation.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Detail the mechanism by which the F0 domain of Complex V (ATP Synthase) facilitates the phosphorylation of ADP within the mitochondrial matrix.
back:
• Acts as a transmembrane proton channel.
• Dissipates the pH gradient by returning protons to the matrix.
• Rotation of F0 induces conformational changes in the F1 sphere.
• Energy is used to bind ADP and Pi.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Contrast the entry points and energy yields of electrons derived from NADH versus those from succinate in the respiratory chain.
back:
• NADH: Enters at Complex I; yields ~3 ATP.
• Succinate: Enters at Complex II via FADH2; yields ~2 ATP.
• Complex II does not pump protons, reducing its P:O ratio.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Identify the lipid-soluble, mobile electron carrier that collects reducing equivalents from both Complex I and Complex II to deliver them to Complex III.
back:
Coenzyme Q (Ubiquinone).
• A non-protein quinone derivative.
• Shuttles electrons within the lipid bilayer.
• Essential link between flavoproteins and cytochromes.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: The small peripheral heme protein that shuttles single electrons from Complex III to the terminal cytochrome oxidase complex is [___].
back:
Cytochrome c.
• Located on the outer face of the inner membrane.
• Reversibly converts between Fe3+ and Fe2+ states.
• Crucial mediator in the intrinsic apoptosis pathway.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: A laboratory mitochondrial suspension stops oxygen consumption when Rotenone is added, but respiration resumes upon adding succinate. Identify the specific blocked site.
back:
Complex I (NADH Dehydrogenase).
• Rotenone specifically blocks the NADH-to-CoQ transfer.
• Succinate bypasses the block by entering through Complex II.
• Demonstrates the independence of entry pathways.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Explain the role of copper atoms (CuA and CuB) in the final reduction of molecular oxygen to water at Complex IV.
back:
• Facilitate the four-electron reduction of O2.
• CuB is associated with the a3 heme group.
• Prevents the release of toxic reactive oxygen species (ROS).
• Essential for the terminal oxidase activity.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Distinguish between the physiological impact of 'uncouplers' like DNP and 'inhibitors' like Cyanide on the rate of oxygen consumption.
back:
• Uncouplers: Dissipate proton gradient; increase oxygen consumption/heat; decrease ATP.
• Inhibitors: Block electron flow; stop oxygen consumption; stop ATP synthesis.
• Uncouplers bypass the respiratory control mechanism.

category: Diagrammatically illustrate the organization of electron transport chain (ETC) depicting the flow of electrons
front: Name the specific mitochondrial enzyme that also functions as Complex II of the electron transport chain, linking the TCA cycle directly to respiration.
back:
Succinate Dehydrogenase.
• Only TCA cycle enzyme embedded in the inner membrane.
• Uses FAD as a prosthetic group.
• Transfers electrons directly to the ubiquinone pool.

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: The initial electron acceptor in Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) which receives a hydride ion from NADH is [___].
back:
FMN (Flavin Mononucleotide)
* It accepts 2 electrons and 2 protons to become FMNH2.
* It then transfers electrons to Iron-Sulfur (Fe-S) centers.

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: A researcher observes that a mitochondrial preparation can oxidize succinate but cannot pump protons at that specific entry point. Identify the enzyme complex and its associated flavin cofactor.
back:
Complex II (Succinate Dehydrogenase)
* Cofactor: FAD (Flavin Adenine Dinucleotide)
* Function: Transfers electrons from succinate to CoQ via Fe-S centers.

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: Describe the electron transfer pathway through the specific cytochromes located within Complex III.
back:
Electrons move from CoQH2 to:
* Cytochrome b (bL and bH)
* Rieske Iron-Sulfur (Fe-S) center
* Cytochrome c1

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: Contrast the metallic centers of Complex III with those of Complex IV regarding their non-heme components.
back:
Complex III: Contains Rieske Iron-Sulfur (Fe-S) centers.
* Complex IV: Contains Copper centers (CuA and CuB).

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: Enlist the specific cytochromes and ions required for the final reduction of oxygen to water in Complex IV.
back:
Cytochrome a and Cytochrome a3
* Copper ions (CuA and CuB)
* Heme iron (Fe2+/Fe3+)

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: In the respiratory chain, the complex also known as Cytochrome bc1 is [___].
back:
Complex III
* Contains: Cytochrome b, Cytochrome c1, and Fe-S protein.
* Role: Pumps 4 protons per pair of electrons.

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: A patient is exposed to Carbon Monoxide (CO). Identify the specific complex inhibited and the cytochromes that lose the ability to react with oxygen.
back:
Complex IV (Cytochrome oxidase)
* Inhibited Cytochromes: a and a3
* Mechanism: CO binds to the heme iron of Cytochrome a3.

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: Explain the role of the Rieske protein during the Q-cycle in Complex III.
back:
It is an Iron-Sulfur (2Fe-2S) protein.
* It accepts one electron from ubiquinol (CoQH2).
* It then transfers that electron to Cytochrome c1.

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: Distinguish between Complex I and Complex II based on their interaction with the mitochondrial matrix protons.
back:
Complex I: Pumps 4 protons into the intermembrane space.
* Complex II: Does not pump any protons (lacks enough free energy).

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: Name the four protein complexes of the electron transport chain that are embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
back:
Complex I (NADH Dehydrogenase)
* Complex II (Succinate Dehydrogenase)
* Complex III (Cytochrome bc1)
* Complex IV (Cytochrome oxidase)

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: In the mitochondrial respiratory chain, the primary prosthetic group of Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) that accepts hydride ions is [___].
back:
- Flavin Mononucleotide (FMN)
- Receives 2 electrons from NADH
- Transfers electrons to Iron-Sulfur (Fe-S) centers

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: A 15-year-old male with exercise intolerance is found to have a defect in the mitochondrial enzyme that bridges the TCA cycle and ETC. This complex contains [___].
back:
- Flavin Adenine Dinucleotide (FAD)
- Iron-Sulfur (Fe-S) clusters
- Part of Succinate Dehydrogenase (Complex II)

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: Describe the specific arrangement of electron carriers within Complex III (Cytochrome bc1 complex).
back:
- Cytochrome b (hemes bL and bH)
- Cytochrome c1
- Rieske iron-sulfur protein (2Fe-2S center)

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: Contrast the prosthetic group used for the initial electron capture in Complex I versus Complex II.
back:
- Complex I: Uses Flavin Mononucleotide (FMN)
- Complex II: Uses Flavin Adenine Dinucleotide (FAD)
- Both eventually transfer electrons to Ubiquinone (CoQ)

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: Identify the unique metallic centers and cytochromes that constitute Complex IV (Cytochrome c oxidase).
back:
- Cytochromes a and a3
- Two Copper centers (CuA and CuB)
- Reduces molecular oxygen to water

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: The respiratory complex that lacks a proton pump and contains Succinate Dehydrogenase is characterized by its bound [___] coenzyme.
back:
- FAD (Flavin Adenine Dinucleotide)
- Transfers electrons from Succinate to Coenzyme Q
- Contains multiple Fe-S centers

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: A patient presents with metabolic acidosis and "cherry-red" skin after house fire exposure. The toxin binds to the heme iron of [___].
back:
- Complex IV (Cytochrome c Oxidase)
- Specifically binds Cytochromes a/a3
- Halts the final step of electron transport

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: Explain the components of the 'Cytochrome bc1 complex' (Complex III) involved in the Q-cycle.
back:
- Cytochrome b (two heme groups)
- Cytochrome c1
- Rieske iron-sulfur protein (Fe-S center)
- Shuttles electrons to Cytochrome c

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: Contrast the iron-containing proteins found in Complex II with those in Complex III.
back:
- Complex II: Contains Iron-Sulfur (Fe-S) clusters only
- Complex III: Contains both Fe-S clusters and Cytochromes (heme-based)
- Complex III pumps protons; Complex II does not

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: Enlist the prosthetic groups that allow Complex I to function as an NADH:Ubiquinone Oxidoreductase.
back:
- Flavin Mononucleotide (FMN)
- Multiple Iron-Sulfur (Fe-S) centers
- Transfers electrons from NADH to Coenzyme Q

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: In the Mitochondrial Electron Transport Chain, Complex I (NADH Dehydrogenase) accepts electrons from NADH via the prosthetic group [___].
back: • Flavin Mononucleotide (FMN) • FMN is reduced to FMNH2 • It subsequently transfers electrons to multiple Iron-Sulfur (Fe-S) centers.

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: A patient with a mitochondrial disorder shows specific deficiency in the only membrane-bound enzyme of the TCA cycle. Identify this complex and its primary prosthetic group.
back: • Complex II (Succinate Dehydrogenase) • Prosthetic group: FAD (Flavin Adenine Dinucleotide) • Also contains Iron-Sulfur (Fe-S) clusters and Cytochrome b560.

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: Explain the specific role of the Copper centers (CuA and CuB) within the structure of Mitochondrial Complex IV.
back: • CuA: Receives electrons from mobile Cytochrome c • CuB: Works in conjunction with Heme a3 • Together they facilitate the reduction of O2 to H2O.

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: Contrast the prosthetic groups used for initial electron acceptance in Complex I versus Complex II.
back: • Complex I: Uses FMN (Flavin Mononucleotide) • Complex II: Uses FAD (Flavin Adenine Dinucleotide) • Both eventually channel electrons into the Ubiquinone (CoQ) pool.

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: Enlist the three primary protein subunits that constitute the Cytochrome bc1 complex (Complex III).
back: • Cytochrome b (containing hemes bL and bH) • Cytochrome c1 • Rieske Iron-Sulfur protein (2Fe-2S).

category: Enlist the components of complex I, II, III, and IV
front: Complex IV, the terminal oxidase of the respiratory chain, contains two distinct heme-iron centers designated as [___] and [___].
