• BMR is directly proportional to surface area.
• Greater surface area increases heat loss to environment.
• Requires higher metabolic activity to maintain core temperature.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: Contrast Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) with Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR) regarding their respective measurement requirements.
back:
• BMR: Strict 12-hour fast; measured immediately after waking.
• RMR: Less restrictive; no overnight fast required.
• BMR is typically lower due to stricter basal states.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: Identify three essential 'basal conditions' that must be maintained to accurately determine a patient's BMR.
back:
• Post-absorptive state (12–14 hours after last meal).
• Complete physical and mental relaxation.
• Thermoneutral environment to avoid shivering/sweating.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: In clinical metabolic assessment, the most significant hormonal factor responsible for long-term regulation of BMR is [___].
back:
• Thyroid Hormone (Thyroxine/T4).
• Increases Na+/K+ ATPase activity.
• Regulates the basal oxygen consumption of tissues.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: A hospitalized patient develops a high-grade fever. Predict the physiological impact on their Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR).
back:
• BMR increases significantly during fever.
• Accelerates chemical reaction kinetics (Van't Hoff's law).
• Heightens cardiac and respiratory energy demands.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: Describe the physiological mechanism by which prolonged starvation or severe calorie restriction alters the BMR.
back:
• BMR decreases (metabolic adaptation).
• Body conserves energy by reducing lean mass activity.
• Downregulation of sympathetic nervous system and thyroid hormones.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: Distinguish between the BMR of an adult male and an adult female of identical weight and age.
back:
• Males have a higher BMR.
• Driven by greater lean muscle mass proportion.
• Females possess higher fat-to-muscle ratios (fat is metabolically sluggish).

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: State the standard unit used to express Basal Metabolic Rate in clinical practice.
back:
• kcal/square meter of body surface/hour.
• Normal values are roughly 35-40 kcal/m²/hr in adults.
• Declines naturally with advancing age.

category: Outline treatment strategies
front: The pharmacological agent [___] is utilized in peptic ulcer management to specifically inhibit the gastric proton pump (H+K+ ATPase).
back:
• Omeprazole
• Irreversibly binds the H+K+ ATPase pump
• Reduces daily HCl production by up to 95%
• Inhibits the final step of acid secretion.

category: Outline treatment strategies
front: A patient with peptic ulcer disease is treated with Cimetidine. Identify the specific receptor type and cell targeted by this drug strategy.
back:
• H2-histaminergic receptors
• Located on the Parietal (oxyntic) cell
• Blocks histamine-induced acid stimulation
• Other examples include Ranitidine and Famotidine.

category: Outline treatment strategies
front: Describe the multi-level gastric defense mechanisms promoted by Prostaglandin E1 analogs in clinical therapy.
back:
• Increases mucus and HCO3- secretion
• Enhances sub-epithelial microcirculation
• Facilitates epithelial cell restitution (repair)
• Directly inhibits adenylyl cyclase to reduce HCl.

category: Outline treatment strategies
front: Contrast the therapeutic efficacy and mechanisms of Atropine versus Omeprazole in reducing gastric acidity.
back:
• Atropine: Anticholinergic; blocks muscarinic receptors; less effective; more systemic side effects.
• Omeprazole: PPI; blocks the final common H+ pump; more potent acid suppression (95%).

category: Outline treatment strategies
front: Identify the pharmacological rationale for using Proglumide as a treatment strategy for gastrin-dependent hyperacidity.
back:
• Acts as an anti-gastrin substance
• Competes with gastrin for its cellular receptor
• Structural similarity to the terminal gastrin molecule
• Blocks gastrin-mediated parietal and ECL cell stimulation.

category: Outline treatment strategies
front: To prevent dental caries in patients with xerostomia, the primary treatment strategy must address the lack of [___] in the oral cavity.
back:
• Saliva
• Saliva cleanses food residues and bacteria
• Contains Lysozyme (antibacterial)
• Contains secretory IgA and calcium-binding proteins.

category: Outline treatment strategies
front: A patient develops 'Dumping Syndrome' after a partial gastrectomy. Which dietary modification serves as the primary management strategy?
back:
• Reducing hyperosmolar carbohydrate intake
• Prevents rapid osmotic shifts in the small intestine
• Limits local liberation of serotonin and kinins
• Prevents associated weakness and palpitations.

category: Outline treatment strategies
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism of 'Acid Rebound' that complicates the treatment of hyperacidity with large doses of alkaline antacids.
back:
• Neutralization removes the normal acid-inhibitory feedback
• Absence of acid in the antrum triggers Gastrin release
• Gastrin subsequently stimulates a rebound surge of HCl production.

category: Outline treatment strategies
front: Contrast the effects of Acetylcholine versus Secretin on the parietal cell's secretory activity.
back:
• Acetylcholine: Parasympathetic stimulant; increases HCl by metabolic phosphoinositide turnover.
• Secretin: Stimulated by duodenal acid; inhibits gastric HCl; stimulates pancreatic HCO3-.

category: Outline treatment strategies
front: Identify the surgical intervention strategy used to treat refractory peptic ulcers by eliminating the neural phase of secretion.
back:
• Vagotomy
• Sectioning of vagus nerves
• Eliminates acetylcholine-mediated acid stimulation
• Reduces both basal and cephalic phase HCl.

category: Define Malnutrition
front: In clinical nutrition, substances like vitamins and minerals required in small quantities are termed micronutrients, whereas energy-rich molecules such as fats and proteins are called [___].
back: * Macronutrients. * Required in large amounts to provide energy. * Includes fats, carbohydrates, and proteins.

category: Define Malnutrition
front: A 10-month-old infant in a developing country presents with arrested growth, extreme muscle wasting, and a 'skin and bones' appearance. No edema is present. What is the most likely diagnosis?
back: * Marasmus. * Result of chronic deficiency in both protein and total calories. * Occurs typically in children under 1 year of age.

category: Define Malnutrition
front: Explain the biochemical role of plasma proteins in the development of edema in patients with severe Protein-Energy Malnutrition (PEM).
back: * Severe protein deficiency decreases hepatic albumin synthesis. * Reduced plasma albumin lowers intravascular oncotic pressure. * Fluid shifts from the blood into the interstitial space, causing edema.

category: Define Malnutrition
front: Contrast the typical mental state and mood of a child suffering from Kwashiorkor with that of a child suffering from Marasmus.
back: * Kwashiorkor: Patient is typically apathetic, listless, or lethargic. * Marasmus: Patient is usually alert and irritable.

category: Define Malnutrition
front: Identify the primary cause of Protein-Energy Malnutrition (PEM) in developed countries versus its etiology in developing nations.
back: * Developed: Secondary to medical conditions (e.g., cancer, trauma, malabsorption) or anorexia. * Developing: Primary dietary scarcity of food.

category: Define Malnutrition
front: The metabolic state where the amount of nitrogen intake in the diet is exactly equal to the nitrogen excreted in urine and feces is defined as [___].
back: * Nitrogen Balance. * Observed in healthy adults. * Reflects a steady state of protein synthesis and degradation.

category: Define Malnutrition
front: A 45-year-old patient suffering from severe third-degree burns is likely to exhibit which specific nitrogen balance status?
back: * Negative Nitrogen Balance. * Excretion of nitrogen exceeds intake. * Caused by increased tissue protein breakdown due to metabolic stress.

category: Define Malnutrition
front: Describe the physiological impact of severe Protein-Energy Malnutrition (PEM) on the immune system and its consequences.
back: * Depresses the immune system. * Reduces the body's ability to resist infection. * Leads to increased mortality from secondary infections.

category: Define Malnutrition
front: Distinguish between the standard metabolic caloric values (kcal/g) provided by dietary fats versus dietary proteins.
back: * Fats: Provide 9 kcal/g. * Proteins: Provide 4 kcal/g. * Fats are more than twice as energy-dense as proteins or carbohydrates.

category: Define Malnutrition
front: List three specific physiological states or life stages that necessitate an increase in dietary protein intake to achieve a positive nitrogen balance.
back: * 1. Pregnancy. * 2. Lactation. * 3. Childhood/Growth. * 4. Recovery from emaciating illness.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: To ensure a strictly post-absorptive state for accurate measurement of Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR), the patient must have fasted for [___] hours.
back:
• 12 to 14 hours.
• Prevents the influence of Specific Dynamic Action (SDA) of food.
• Ensures metabolism is at the base maintenance level.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: A 35-year-old female presents with heat intolerance, tremors, and weight loss. Her Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) is found to be +60%. Identify the underlying hormonal cause and its effect on cellular oxygen consumption.
back:
• Hyperthyroidism (Excess T3/T4).
• Increases mitochondrial oxygen consumption.
• Upregulates Na+-K+ ATPase activity, accelerating metabolic heat production.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: Explain the biological rationale for why Basal Metabolic Rate is expressed per unit of body surface area rather than total body weight.
back:
• Heat loss occurs primarily through the skin.
• Heat loss is proportional to surface area.
• Ensures a standard comparison between individuals of different heights and weights.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: Contrast the physiological impact of prolonged starvation versus an acute febrile illness on the Basal Metabolic Rate.
back:
• Starvation: Decreases BMR (adaptive conservation of energy and tissue).
• Fever: Increases BMR (approx. 12% per 1°C rise).
• Starvation reduces active protoplasmic mass; fever accelerates enzymatic reaction rates.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: Identify the primary hormone responsible for maintaining BMR and its specific mechanism in increasing mitochondrial thermogenesis.
back:
• Thyroxine (T4/T3).
• Increases the number and activity of mitochondria.
• Stimulates uncoupling proteins and ATP-consuming pumps.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: In the clinical estimation of energy expenditure, the standard indirect calorimetry apparatus utilized to measure oxygen consumption for BMR calculation is the [___].
back:
• Benedict-Roth apparatus.
• Measures oxygen consumed over a set period.
• Oxygen consumption is then converted to kilocalories.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: A 60-year-old male with chronic renal failure exhibits significant muscle wasting. Explain the likely shift in his BMR and the status of his nitrogen balance.
back:
• BMR decreases due to loss of metabolically active muscle mass.
• Negative nitrogen balance exists.
• Protein catabolism exceeds intake, reducing the total energy required for maintenance.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: Detail the mechanism by which the 'Specific Dynamic Action' (SDA) of protein increases total metabolic expenditure beyond the basal rate.
back:
• Protein has an SDA of 30%.
• Energy is consumed for deamination of amino acids.
• Energy is required for urea synthesis and protein turnover.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: Distinguish between the BMR of adult males and females, specifically regarding the influence of lean body mass.
back:
• Males: 5–10% higher BMR due to greater muscle mass.
• Females: Lower BMR due to higher percentage of adipose tissue.
• Muscle is more metabolically active than fat.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: State the average BMR value for a healthy adult male in terms of kilocalories per square meter of body surface per hour.
back:
• 35–40 kcal/sq.m/hour.
• Roughly 1,600 kcal/day for a 70 kg man.
• Decreases with age due to muscle loss.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: The single most significant hormonal regulator of BMR, which increases oxygen consumption and heat production in almost all body tissues, is [___].
back:
* Thyroxine (T4) / Triiodothyronine (T3)
* Stimulates cellular oxidative metabolism
* Increases mitochondrial activity and Na+-K+ ATPase pumps

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: A patient with enteric fever presents with a temperature of 104°F. Describe the expected change in their Basal Metabolic Rate relative to their body temperature rise.
back:
* BMR increases significantly
* Typically rises ~12% to 13% for every 1°C increase
* Result of accelerated intracellular chemical reactions

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Explain how body surface area (BSA) influences the Basal Metabolic Rate in adults of different statures.
back:
* BMR is directly proportional to BSA
* Greater BSA leads to higher heat loss through the skin
* Requires more metabolic energy to maintain core temperature

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Contrast the physiological shift in BMR observed during prolonged starvation versus the state of late-term pregnancy.
back:
* Starvation: BMR decreases (~10-20%) to conserve energy stores
* Pregnancy: BMR increases (~15-20%) due to fetal growth and uterine metabolism
* Starvation involves adaptive hypometabolism

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Describe the general trend of Basal Metabolic Rate from infancy through geriatric age groups.
back:
* Highest in infancy and childhood (rapid growth phase)
* Gradually declines throughout adult life
* Reduction linked to loss of lean muscle mass in elderly

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Women generally exhibit a BMR approximately 5-10% lower than men of the same weight and height due to a higher physiological proportion of [___].
back:
* Adipose tissue (Fat)
* Fat is metabolically less active than skeletal muscle
* Men possess higher lean body mass (LBM)

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: A 45-year-old female presents with cold intolerance, significant weight gain despite low appetite, and bradycardia. Identify the pathological effect on her BMR.
back:
* Severely decreased BMR
* Characteristic of Hypothyroidism (Myxedema)
* Result of decreased metabolic rate in all cells

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Explain the metabolic adjustment of BMR in individuals residing in extremely cold polar climates compared to those in tropical regions.
back:
* Higher BMR in cold climates
* Increased thyroxine secretion to maintain homeothermy
* Tropical residents show lower BMR due to reduced thermogenic need

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Distinguish between the BMR measured during a state of wakeful rest and the metabolic rate recorded during deep sleep.
back:
* Sleep BMR is approximately 10% lower
* Attributed to complete skeletal muscle relaxation
* Lowered sympathetic nervous system tone during sleep

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: State the standard environmental and physiological conditions required to accurately measure a patient's Basal Metabolic Rate.
back:
* Post-absorptive state (12-14 hour fast)
* Complete mental and physical relaxation
* Thermoneutral environment (Comfortable room temperature)

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: The primary endocrine regulator of BMR is thyroxine, which elevates oxygen consumption by inducing the synthesis of [___] in almost all nucleated cells.
back:
• Na+/K+ ATPase pumps
• Increases ATP consumption
• Stimulates cellular respiration and heat production

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: A 28-year-old female presents with tremors, heat intolerance, and exophthalmos. Clinical assessment would reveal an [___] BMR due to hyperthyroidism.
back:
• Increased BMR
• Excessive T3/T4 levels stimulate metabolic pathways
• Often exceeds 50-100% above normal baselines

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Explain the mechanism by which prolonged starvation or severe caloric restriction leads to a reduction in Basal Metabolic Rate.
back:
• Conservation mechanism to preserve energy
• Decreased lean body mass
• Reduced conversion of T4 to active T3

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Contrast the influence of lean muscle mass versus adipose tissue on the total BMR of an individual.
back:
• Muscle: Metabolically active tissue; significantly increases BMR
• Fat: Relatively inert storage tissue; contributes minimally to BMR

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: State the relationship established by Rubner's Law between body surface area and metabolic rate.
back:
• BMR is directly proportional to surface area
• Taller, thinner individuals lose more heat
• Higher BMR required to maintain core temperature

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: In pathological states such as fever, the BMR [___] significantly due to the Van't Hoff effect on chemical reaction rates.
back:
• Increases
• Metabolic rate rises with core temperature
• Increased enzymatic activity and cardiac workload

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: A 70-year-old patient exhibits a lower BMR compared to their 25-year-old self. This physiological decline is primarily due to [___].
back:
• Loss of lean muscle (Sarcopenia)
• Increased proportion of body fat
• Reduced hormonal activity and protein turnover

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Explain why infants and growing children exhibit the highest BMR when measured per unit of body weight.
back:
• High rate of protein synthesis/growth
• Increased secretion of Growth Hormone
• Larger surface area-to-body weight ratio

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Contrast the BMR changes observed in the physiological state of pregnancy versus a standard adult female.
back:
• Pregnancy: BMR increases (late stages)
• Cause: Metabolic activity of the fetus/placenta
• Increased maternal cardiac and respiratory workload

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Identify the primary physiological reason why males generally possess a BMR 5–10% higher than females of the same age and height.
back:
• Higher lean muscle mass
• Lower percentage of body fat
• Anabolic effects of testosterone

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: In relation to body size, individuals with a larger [___] tend to have a significantly higher Basal Metabolic Rate due to increased heat loss.
back:
* Body Surface Area (BSA).
* Large BSA increases heat dissipation to the environment.
* Increases metabolic heat production to maintain core temperature.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: A 45-year-old patient presents with heat intolerance, weight loss despite increased appetite, and tachycardia. In this patient, the BMR is expected to [___].
back:
* Increase significantly.
* Likely due to Hyperthyroidism.
* Thyroid hormones stimulate mitochondrial respiration and Na+/K+ ATPase activity.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Explain the physiological reason why males generally exhibit a 5-10% higher BMR compared to females of the same age and weight.
back:
* Higher lean muscle mass in males.
* Muscle is metabolically more active than adipose tissue.
* Higher testosterone levels promote protein synthesis and metabolic rate.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Contrast the adaptive effect of prolonged starvation on BMR with the metabolic effect of an acute febrile illness.
back:
* Starvation: Decreases BMR to conserve energy stores.
* Fever: Increases BMR (~12% per 1°C rise).
* Starvation involves downregulated thyroid activity; fever involves cytokine-mediated acceleration.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
coreConcept: Age as a factor in BMR
front: Describe the relationship between advancing age and Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) from infancy through late adulthood.
back:
* Highest BMR per unit weight during infancy/childhood.
* Gradual decline in adulthood (~2% per decade).
* Decline linked to muscle atrophy and reduced cellular metabolic activity.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: The pathological state characterized by cold intolerance, weight gain, and a significantly [___] Basal Metabolic Rate is Hypothyroidism.
back:
* Decreased (lowered).
* Result of reduced cellular oxygen consumption.
* Downregulation of mitochondrial respiratory enzymes due to low T3/T4.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: A woman in her third trimester of pregnancy is being assessed for nutritional needs. How does her physiological state impact her Basal Metabolic Rate?
back:
* Increases BMR (approx. 15-25%).
* Driven by the metabolic demands of the growing fetus.
* Increased workload on maternal cardiac and respiratory systems.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: How does residence in an extremely cold climate physiologically influence an individual's BMR compared to a tropical environment?
back:
* BMR increases in cold climates.
* Mechanism: Shivering and non-shivering thermogenesis.
* Increased thyroxine secretion to maintain body heat.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Contrast the Basal Metabolic Rate measured during deep sleep with the BMR measured during the standard waking, resting state.
back:
* Sleep: BMR decreases by approx. 10-15%.
* Waking: Baseline 'basal' level is higher.
* Reduction during sleep is due to skeletal muscle relaxation.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Identify the hormone primarily responsible for the long-term physiological regulation of the Basal Metabolic Rate in healthy individuals.
back:
* Thyroxine (T4/T3).
* Increases basal oxygen consumption across most tissues.
* Enhances mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: The [___] state, occurring 12 hours after the last meal in a thermoneutral environment, is the mandatory condition for measuring Basal Metabolic Rate.
back:
• Post-absorptive state
• Ensures absence of digestive activity
• Requires physical and mental rest
• Prevents metabolic interference from food.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: A 25-year-old male with Hyperthyroidism presents with a significantly elevated Basal Metabolic Rate. This increase is primarily due to the [___] effect of thyroid hormones.
back:
• Calorigenic effect
• Stimulates Na+/K+ ATPase activity
• Increases mitochondrial oxygen consumption
• Enhances overall cellular metabolism.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: Explain the role of lean body mass (LBM) as the most significant predictor of an individual's Basal Metabolic Rate.
back:
• LBM is metabolically active tissue
• Higher mitochondrial density than fat
• Increases energy demand for protein turnover
• Accounts for most BMR variance.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: Contrast the Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) with the Thermic Effect of Food (TEF) regarding their contribution to Total Energy Expenditure (TEE).
back:
• BMR: Energy for vital functions (60–75% TEE)
• TEF: Energy for digestion/absorption (5–10% TEE)
• BMR is measured while fasting
• TEF is induced by meal ingestion.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: Why does the Basal Metabolic Rate typically decrease by approximately 2% per decade after the age of 30?
back:
• Loss of lean muscle mass (Sarcopenia)
• Increase in relative adipose tissue
• Reduction in cellular protein synthesis
• Decreased overall organ work.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: To accurately measure BMR, the environmental temperature must be maintained in the [___] to prevent energy expenditure for thermoregulation.
back:
• Thermoneutral zone (Zone of comfort)
• Prevents shivering (heat production)
• Prevents sweating/vasodilation (energy use)
• Ensures minimal metabolic work.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: A patient on a prolonged starvation diet shows a significant drop in BMR. Identify the physiological benefit of this adaptive thermogenesis.
back:
• Energy conservation
• Reduced sympathetic nervous system activity
• Lowered heart rate and respiratory rate
• Preservation of vital organ function.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: How do catecholamines (Epinephrine/Norepinephrine) acutely modify energy expenditure in response to cold or stress?
back:
• Increase BMR via Glycogenolysis
• Stimulate Lipolysis in adipose tissue
• Activate uncoupling proteins (UCPs)
• Direct stimulation of cellular respiration.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: Distinguish between BMR and Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR) regarding clinical measurement protocols.
back:
• BMR: Strict (fasting, overnight stay, awake)
• RMR: Less restrictive (no overnight stay)
• BMR is always slightly lower than RMR
• RMR is more commonly used clinically.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: Identify the gender-based difference in BMR between an average male and female of the same weight.
back:
• Males have 5–10% higher BMR
• Higher muscle-to-fat ratio in males
• Testosterone promotes lean tissue mass
• Females have higher essential fat percentage.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: The [___] is defined as the minimum amount of energy required by an individual in a resting, post-absorptive state to maintain essential life-sustaining functions.
back:
• Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR).
• Measured under strict conditions: physical/mental rest and 12-14 hours post-meal.
• Sustains functions like breathing, circulation, and ion transport.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: A 45-year-old male with untreated hyperthyroidism reports significant weight loss despite increased appetite. Explain the metabolic basis regarding his BMR.
back:
• Elevated thyroid hormones (T3/T4) directly increase BMR.
• Basal oxygen consumption and heat production rise significantly.
• Increased energy expenditure exceeds caloric intake, causing weight loss.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: Explain the role of lean body mass (LBM) in determining an individual's basal metabolic rate.
back:
• Muscle tissue is more metabolically active than adipose tissue.
• Higher LBM increases BMR significantly.
• Explains why males generally have higher BMRs than females.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: Contrast Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) with Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR) regarding their specific measurement conditions.
back:
• BMR: Requires total rest, thermoneutral environment, and strict 12-hour fast.
• RMR: Measured under less restrictive conditions (resting but not total fast).
• RMR is typically slightly higher than BMR.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: Identify the primary cellular mechanism that consumes the largest portion of energy during a basal metabolic state.
back:
• Active ion transport (Na+/K+ ATPase pump).
• Maintenance of electrochemical gradients across cell membranes.
• Protein synthesis and turnover also contribute significantly.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: For an accurate BMR measurement, the patient must be in a [___] state, ensuring no energy is spent on the thermic effect of food.
back:
• Post-absorptive state.
• Requires a minimum of 12 hours since the last meal.
• Eliminates metabolic work associated with digestion and absorption.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: A clinician notes that a patient’s caloric needs have decreased as they transitioned from age 20 to 70. State the primary physiological driver of this BMR change.
back:
• Loss of lean muscle mass (sarcopenia) with aging.
• Increase in relative proportion of fat tissue.
• General decline in cellular metabolic activity and organ efficiency.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: Explain the adaptive metabolic response of BMR during prolonged starvation or chronic caloric restriction.
back:
• BMR decreases to conserve energy.
• Mediated by decreased thyroid hormone (T3) levels.
• Adaptive mechanism to preserve essential body proteins and prolong survival.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: Distinguish between the BMR of a patient with a high fever versus a patient in a cold environment (shivering).
back:
• Fever: BMR increases by approximately 12% per 1°C rise due to accelerated chemical reactions.
• Cold/Shivering: Increases heat production via muscular activity, effectively raising total energy expenditure.

category: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR)
front: Name the three internal organ systems that contribute the most to the BMR in a resting adult despite their small relative weight.
back:
• Liver (highest metabolic contributor).
• Brain.
• Heart and Kidneys.
• These organs have high oxygen consumption per gram of tissue.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: According to Rubner's Surface Area Law, the BMR is directly proportional to the [___] rather than the total body weight.
back:
• Body Surface Area (BSA)
• Larger BSA results in higher heat loss
• Requires higher metabolic activity to maintain body temperature.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: A 35-year-old female presents with weight loss, heat intolerance, and tremors. Her BMR is significantly elevated due to the stimulatory effect of [___] on cellular oxygen consumption.
back:
• Thyroid Hormones (T3 and T4)
• Increases mitochondrial Na+-K+ ATPase activity
• Enhances uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation
• Increases overall cellular thermogenesis.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Explain why measurement of the BMR requires the patient to be in a "post-absorptive state" (12 hours after the last meal).
back:
• Eliminates Specific Dynamic Action (SDA) of food
• SDA is the energy cost of digestion/absorption
• Prevents temporary metabolic spikes during nutrient processing.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Contrast the adaptive BMR changes in a patient with prolonged starvation versus a patient with acute septicemia and high-grade fever.
back:
• Starvation: BMR decreases to conserve lean mass and energy
• Fever: BMR increases significantly
• Pyrexia accelerates enzymatic reaction rates and metabolic turnover.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Describe the influence of acute epinephrine secretion during stress on a patient's basal energy expenditure.
back:
• Increases BMR via β-adrenergic stimulation
• Enhances glycogenolysis and lipolysis
• Rapidly stimulates cellular metabolic rate via cAMP second messenger system.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Females generally exhibit a BMR approximately 5–10% lower than males of the same age and height due to a higher proportion of [___].
back:
• Adipose tissue (Fat)
• Adipose is metabolically less active than muscle
• Males have higher Lean Body Mass (LBM).

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: A patient with myxedema presents with lethargy, cold intolerance, and weight gain. Identify the expected BMR status and the underlying metabolic deficit.
back:
• Status: Decreased BMR (Hypometabolism)
• Cause: Thyroxine deficiency (Hypothyroidism)
• Result: Reduced cellular oxidation and heat production.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Analyze the biochemical mechanism by which a rise in body temperature (Fever) elevates the BMR.
back:
• Q10 Effect: Temperature increases chemical kinetic energy
• Accelerates enzymatic pathways and catalytic turnover
• Increases cardiac and respiratory work-load.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Contrast the BMR requirements of an infant with that of a 70-year-old elderly individual.
back:
• Infants: High BMR due to rapid growth/cell division
• Elderly: Lower BMR due to sarcopenia (muscle loss)
• Decreased lean body mass reduces metabolic demand.

category: Elaborate the effect of various physiological and pathological factors on BMR
front: Identify the impact of living in a cold climate versus a tropical climate on basal metabolic activity.
back:
• Cold: BMR increases to maintain core temperature
• Stimulates shivering and non-shivering thermogenesis
• Tropical: BMR is relatively lower.

category: Clearly differentiate between upper body obesity and lower body obesity
front: The pattern of fat distribution characterized by accumulation in the abdominal region, often associated with a high waist-to-hip ratio, is termed [___] obesity.
back:
Android (Upper Body/Apple-shaped) obesity.
- Involves visceral fat depots.
- Highly associated with metabolic syndrome.
- Carries significantly higher risk for CHD and Type 2 Diabetes.

category: Clearly differentiate between upper body obesity and lower body obesity
coreConcept: Metabolic Risks of Upper Body Obesity
front: A 45-year-old male with a waist circumference of 105 cm presents with hyperinsulinemia and hypertension. Identify the most likely metabolic consequence of this specific fat distribution.
back:
Insulin Resistance.
- Visceral fat is more lipolytically active.
- Releases excess free fatty acids (FFAs) into portal circulation.
- FFAs induce hepatic insulin resistance and gluconeogenesis.

category: Clearly differentiate between upper body obesity and lower body obesity
front: Explain the biochemical difference between visceral adipocytes and gluteal adipocytes regarding catecholamine-induced lipolysis.
back:
Visceral adipocytes are more sensitive.
- They have a higher density of ̢-adrenergic receptors.
- Gluteal fat is metabolically stable with lower lipolysis rates.
- Results in higher FFA flux to the liver in upper body obesity.

category: Clearly differentiate between upper body obesity and lower body obesity
front: Contrast the drainage of lipolysis products between upper body (abdominal) fat and lower body (subcutaneous) fat.
back:
Upper drains to Portal vein; Lower to Systemic.
- Abdominal FFAs directly reach the liver, altering glucose and lipid metabolism.
- Gluteal/femoral FFAs enter systemic circulation, bypassing initial hepatic impact.

category: Clearly differentiate between upper body obesity and lower body obesity
front: Identify the fat distribution pattern typically observed in females that is associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular disease.
back:
Gynoid (Lower Body/Pear-shaped) obesity.
- Fat accumulates in gluteal and femoral regions.
- Primarily subcutaneous rather than visceral.
- Benign metabolic profile compared to android obesity.

category: Clearly differentiate between upper body obesity and lower body obesity
front: In the clinical assessment of regional fat distribution, a Waist-to-Hip Ratio (WHR) exceeding [___] in men is diagnostic of android obesity.
back:
1.0 (WHR >0.8 in women).
- WHR is a better predictor of metabolic risk than BMI.
- Higher ratio indicates centralized visceral fat accumulation.

category: Clearly differentiate between upper body obesity and lower body obesity
front: A female patient with fat accumulation restricted to her hips and thighs shows normal blood glucose and lipid profiles. Determine the clinical significance of this finding.
back:
Lower Metabolic Risk.
- Gynoid fat stores are more stable.
- Less associated with dyslipidemia and insulin resistance.
- Subcutaneous depots act as 'metabolic sinks' for fat storage.

category: Clearly differentiate between upper body obesity and lower body obesity
front: Describe the link between centralized fat depots and the development of pro-inflammatory states in android obesity.
back:
Adipokine secretion.
- Visceral fat secretes pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-̱, IL-6).
- Decreases secretion of adiponectin (insulin-sensitizing hormone).
- Promotes systemic low-grade inflammation and atherosclerosis.

category: Clearly differentiate between upper body obesity and lower body obesity
front: Distinguish between the impact of upper and lower body obesity on hepatic VLDL synthesis.
back:
Upper body obesity increases VLDL.
- High FFA flux from visceral lipolysis to the liver.
- FFAs are re-esterified into triacylglycerols.
- Leads to hypertriglyceridemia and decreased HDL.

category: Clearly differentiate between upper body obesity and lower body obesity
front: Name the specific anatomical fat depot that carries the highest risk for developing Coronary Heart Disease (CHD).
back:
Visceral (Intra-abdominal) fat.
- Closely correlates with high waist circumference.
- Triggers metabolic syndrome triad.
- Major driver of premature cardiovascular mortality.

category: Define body mass index (BMI)
front: The Body Mass Index (BMI) is calculated as weight in kilograms divided by [___].
back: Height in meters squared (m²).

category: Define body mass index (BMI)
front: A 25-year-old female presents with a weight of 85 kg and a height of 1.75 m (BMI ≈ 27.7 kg/m²). Identify the correct WHO weight classification for this patient.
back: Overweight (Range: 25.0 – 29.9 kg/m²).

category: Define body mass index (BMI)
front: How does the Body Mass Index (BMI) function as a surrogate marker for the biological assessment of adipose tissue stores?
back: • Correlates with total body fat in non-athletes. • Provides a standardized metric to screen for health risks associated with excess adiposity (e.g., cardiovascular disease).

category: Define body mass index (BMI)
front: Contrast the clinical utility of Body Mass Index (BMI) with Waist Circumference in a patient with a BMI of 28 kg/m².
back: • BMI: Measures total body mass relative to height. • Waist Circumference: Better indicator of central/visceral fat, which is more metabolically active and dangerous than total mass.

category: Define body mass index (BMI)
front: Identify the specific Body Mass Index (BMI) threshold used to diagnose "Morbid Obesity" (Class III Obesity).
back: BMI ≥ 40.0 kg/m².

category: Define body mass index (BMI)
front: In the WHO classification of weight status, an adult with a Body Mass Index (BMI) between 35.0 and 39.9 kg/m² is categorized as [___].
back: Obesity Class II.

category: Define body mass index (BMI)
front: A muscular 30-year-old male has a BMI of 31 kg/m² but low subcutaneous fat. Why is BMI an inappropriate diagnostic tool for assessing his metabolic risk?
back: • BMI does not distinguish between lean muscle and fat tissue. • Muscular individuals have high mass-to-height ratios without the inflammatory risks of adipose tissue.

category: Define body mass index (BMI)
front: Explain the physiological link between a high BMI and the development of insulin resistance in the metabolic storage pathway.
back: • High BMI reflects expanded adipose tissue. • Excessive adipocytes release free fatty acids and pro-inflammatory cytokines. • These molecules impair insulin receptor signaling in skeletal muscle and liver.

category: Define body mass index (BMI)
front: Contrast the BMI classifications for "Normal Weight" and "Underweight" individuals according to UHS standards.
back: • Underweight: BMI < 18.5 kg/m². • Normal: BMI 18.5 – 24.9 kg/m².

category: Define body mass index (BMI)
front: State the primary clinical drawback of using BMI to assess nutritional status in patients with chronic liver disease and ascites.
back: • Weight is falsely elevated due to fluid retention (edema/ascites). • BMI may mask severe underlying muscle wasting and malnutrition.
